title: Grade 1 daily reading
overview: An adult reads authentic poems, fables, fantasy, legends, and historical nature prose across 180 evenings. Children respond orally, join refrains in shared readings, and revisit exact words. Suggested 10–15-minute sessions include rereading and three text-specific conversations; they do not assume independent decoding of historical vocabulary. The year moves from noticing patterns to remembering longer arcs, distinguishing observation from invention, and supporting interpretations. Historical myths and legends are identified as stories, and the nature excerpts distinguish figurative language and dated terminology from observation.

progression.focus: Hear patterns, notice details, and retell a short sequence.
progression.rationale: Adult reading and rereading make authentic verse, fables, and tales available while children join refrains, connect two events, and point to a spoken phrase.

progression.focus: Connect choices to consequences and compare different helpers.
progression.rationale: Longer linked scenes ask listeners to remember an earlier problem and distinguish what each character contributes. An adult recaps and rereads evidence.

progression.focus: Follow a continuing adventure and explain changes in a character.
progression.rationale: Several consecutive excerpts preserve the story’s arc. Children increasingly select details to explain a guess, while poems interrupt longer narrative runs.

progression.focus: Distinguish an imaginative explanation from an observation.
progression.rationale: Nature prose and literary myths invite questions about what can be observed and what the writer invents, without treating historical science as current authority.

progression.focus: Hear different voices and consider more than one interpretation.
progression.rationale: Dialogue, religious legend, and comic adventures stretch memory and inference. Discussion accepts differing readings when the child can connect them to words in the text.

progression.focus: Support an interpretation and connect form with meaning.
progression.rationale: Children take more initiative in finding a telling detail, comparing a beginning with an ending, or explaining how repetition or a narrator’s choice shapes a response. Adults still carry the reading load.

days.title: The forgotten present — opening

days.title: The Skin Horse explains Real — excerpt

days.title: A place beside the Boy — excerpt

days.title: A promise for Eeyore — excerpt

questions.prompt: Why does Pooh stop following Owl’s explanation carefully?

days.title: A familiar bell-rope — excerpt
days.challenge: Use an object’s appearance and history to solve a small mystery.
days.focus: Hear a phrase that means both physically joined and emotionally fond.

days.title: Belling the Cat

days.title: Planning for a Heffalump — excerpt
days.challenge: Notice questions that expose holes in a plan.
days.focus: Compare useful reasoning with guesses based on one’s own tastes.
days.context: After Christopher Robin mentions a Heffalump, Pooh and Piglet decide to catch one though they scarcely know what it is.
days.contentNote: The animal-trap plan is fantasy, not a practical activity.

excerpt.locator: Winnie-the-Pooh, Chapter V; begins “One day, when Christopher Robin and Winnie-the-Pooh and Piglet …” and ends “"Very well," said Pooh, and he stumped off.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Piglet quiet when Pooh first proposes catching a Heffalump?
facilitatorNotes: He wishes he had thought of the idea first; silence here does not simply mean agreement or fear.
evidence: Piglet was wishing that he had thought about it first.

questions.prompt: How does Piglet’s question about rain make Pooh change his account?
facilitatorNotes: Pooh first imagines looking up to ask whether rain is coming, then imagines looking up to ask whether it will stop.
evidence: supposing it were raining already?

questions.prompt: Why does Piglet finally prefer honey to acorns?

days.title: The missing honey — excerpt
days.challenge: Remember an earlier action that the character has forgotten.
days.focus: Find humor in an excuse that disguises wanting a treat.
days.context: Pooh is supplying honey for the friends’ trap. The scene follows the jar from his cupboard to the pit and back into his thoughts.

excerpt.locator: Winnie-the-Pooh, Chapter V; begins “As soon as he got home, he went to …” and ends “… pushed his head right in, and began to lick....”.

questions.prompt: Why does Pooh keep tasting farther down the jar?

evidence: somebody put cheese in at the bottom just for a joke

questions.prompt: Why can the listener explain the empty cupboard before Pooh can?
facilitatorNotes: We have followed the jar to the trap; Pooh forgets what he did with it until the song helps him remember.
evidence: He had put it into the Cunning Trap to catch the Heffalump.

questions.prompt: Why does counting Heffalumps make sleep harder instead of easier?
facilitatorNotes: Each imagined animal eats his honey, making him hungry and worried about losing it.

days.title: The enormous head in the pit — excerpt
days.challenge: Compare what the narrator shows with a frightened character’s interpretation.
days.focus: Trace fear through mixed-up words toward a harmless explanation.
days.context: Pooh has gone into the pit to lick the honey jar. Piglet arrives without knowing this.
days.contentNote: A toy bear is briefly trapped by a jar and freed without injury. Piglet is embarrassed; discuss fear without mocking the frightened friend.

questions.prompt: Why does Piglet inspect the trap before the planned meeting?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to know whether to pretend to be ill; he hopes to avoid danger without losing a fine morning.
evidence: he would go back to bed, and if there wasn't, he wouldn't.

questions.prompt: What is really making the roaring sounds that frighten Piglet?
facilitatorNotes: Pooh is struggling with a honey jar stuck on his head.
evidence: Winnie-the-Pooh had been trying to get the honey-jar off his head.

questions.prompt: Which detail in Piglet’s description almost reveals the answer?
facilitatorNotes: He says the great head is like a jar. The listener can connect that clue to the narrator’s explanation.
evidence: Like a jar.

days.title: Hercules and the Waggoner
days.challenge: Follow a problem, an appeal for help, and a concrete instruction.
days.focus: A mythic helper answers with an action the troubled person can take.
days.context: Hercules is a strong figure from Greek myth; mire means mud. The fable’s saying does not mean people who need assistance are undeserving of help.

questions.prompt: Why does the wagon become harder to move?
facilitatorNotes: Its wheels sink in mud; pulling makes them sink more deeply.
evidence: the deeper sank the wheels

questions.prompt: What help does Hercules actually offer in the scene?

evidence: put your shoulder to the wheel

questions.prompt: Does the scene tell us the wagon is finally freed?
facilitatorNotes: No; it ends with advice and a saying. Distinguish an expected result from one the narrator actually reports.

days.title: A birthday nobody noticed — excerpt
days.challenge: Hear the difference between literal words and a sad joke.
days.focus: Recognize a request for attention that is difficult to state directly.
days.context: Pooh finds Eeyore looking at his reflection beside a stream on his birthday.

questions.prompt: Why does moving to the other bank fail to improve Eeyore’s reflection?
facilitatorNotes: The sad donkey is still seeing himself; changing sides does not change his feeling of neglect.
evidence: No better from this side.

evidence: Neither can I

questions.prompt: What makes Pooh stop singing and take action?
facilitatorNotes: He learns Eeyore’s birthday has passed without attention and hurries to find a gift.
evidence: he felt that he must get poor Eeyore a present of some sort at once

days.title: A useful pot and wobbly spelling — excerpt
days.challenge: Track how an intended gift changes through a character’s mistake.
days.focus: Compare a sincere intention with imperfect delivery.
days.context: Pooh wants to cheer Eeyore with honey, and Piglet chooses a balloon.

facilitatorNotes: The honey is Eeyore’s present; he remembers only when the jar is empty.
evidence: He had eaten Eeyore's birthday present!

facilitatorNotes: He decides the clean pot can store things, turning an empty container into a gift.
evidence: Eeyore could keep things in it

questions.prompt: Does Owl’s long inscription prove he spells better than Pooh?
facilitatorNotes: No; the visible letters do not spell the claimed greeting. An adult can read the intended phrase without demanding decoding of nonsense.
evidence: HIPY PAPY BTHUTHDTH THUTHDA BTHUTHDY.

days.title: Piglet’s burst balloon — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow imagined explanations before the actual cause is found.
days.focus: Read disappointment together with concern for a friend.
days.context: Piglet runs to give Eeyore the first present, carrying his balloon close to him.

questions.prompt: What distracts Piglet from watching where he is running?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines Eeyore’s pleasure and wants to arrive first.
evidence: thinking how pleased Eeyore would be

questions.prompt: How does his explanation of the bang shrink from enormous to ordinary?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines the world, the forest, or himself exploding before noticing the burst balloon.
evidence: At first he thought that the whole world had blown up

questions.prompt: What does Eeyore ask before hearing the bad news about the balloon?
facilitatorNotes: He asks whether Piglet was hurt, showing care even while expecting a gift.
evidence: You didn't hurt yourself, Little Piglet?

days.title: Two presents that fit together — excerpt
days.challenge: Connect two earlier disappointments to one satisfying ending.
days.focus: Notice a recipient finding pleasure the givers had not predicted.
days.context: Pooh brings an empty pot after eating the honey; Piglet has given Eeyore a burst balloon. Neither present looks as originally planned.

questions.prompt: Why is the repeated moving in and out important rather than just busy action?
facilitatorNotes: It shows Eeyore actively enjoying the gifts, and lets Piglet and Pooh share his pleasure.
evidence: as happy as could be

questions.prompt: How does Christopher Robin’s interruption add something to Eeyore’s birthday?
facilitatorNotes: He supplies a box of paints and remembers preparing a real party with cake and candles.

days.title: Rabbit’s plan about the newcomers — excerpt
days.challenge: Hold the parts of a written plan in mind and notice who doubts it.
days.focus: Rabbit’s numbered plan sounds clever, but the characters’ worries show its flaws before anyone acts.
days.context: Two newcomers, Kanga and her baby Roo, have arrived in the Forest. Rabbit, Pooh and Piglet meet to talk about them. A Kanga is Milne’s word for a kangaroo.
days.contentNote: Rabbit plans to take Baby Roo away and hide him so that Kanga will leave the Forest; the chapter later ends in friendship, and Roo comes to no harm.

excerpt.locator: Winnie-the-Pooh, Chapter VII, from the chapter opening; begins “Nobody seemed to know where they came from, but …” and ends “So they all went out to look for Kanga.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Rabbit unhappy that Kanga and Roo have come to the Forest?
facilitatorNotes: They are strangers he has never heard of, and Kanga carries her family in a pocket. Ask whether being new or different is a good reason to want someone to leave.
evidence: We find a Strange Animal among us.

questions.prompt: What does Rabbit say “Aha!” is supposed to mean?
facilitatorNotes: It is a threat: they will tell Kanga where Roo is only if she promises to leave the Forest. Pooh is not sure the word can mean all that.
evidence: 'Aha!' means 'We'll tell you where Baby Roo is, if you promise to go away from the Forest and never come back.'

questions.prompt: How does Rabbit get Piglet to agree even though Piglet is frightened?
facilitatorNotes: He says a very small animal will be Useful, and that Kangas are only fierce in winter. Piglet’s later question about the winter months shows his worry has not gone.
evidence: It is because you are a very small animal that you will be Useful in the adventure before us.

questions.prompt: According to Rabbit’s written plan, what is Pooh’s job?
facilitatorNotes: To talk to Kanga very excitedly so that she looks the other way while Piglet and Roo change places. Pooh thinks of telling her some poetry.
evidence: But if Pooh was talking to her very excitedly, she might look the other way for a moment.

days.title: A distraction that takes time — excerpt
days.challenge: Track different characters’ intentions in one conversation.
days.focus: Notice a caregiver’s attention and a poorly disguised trick.
days.context: Rabbit, Pooh and Piglet have set out to carry out Rabbit’s plan. Kanga is watching her child closely.
days.contentNote: Friends play an unfair child-swapping trick; no child is harmed, and the later ending reconciles them. Discuss the deception as a bad idea rather than a model for play.

excerpt.locator: Winnie-the-Pooh, Chapter VII; begins “Kanga and Roo were spending a quiet afternoon in …” and ends “… "Ooooooo-ow, Ooooooo-ow, Ooooooo-ow" all the way to Kanga's house.”.

questions.prompt: What does Roo repeatedly want the visitors to watch?
facilitatorNotes: His jumps, even when he tumbles into small holes. His excitement competes with the adults’ talk.
evidence: Look at me jumping

questions.prompt: Why does Pooh’s poem fail to turn Kanga’s attention away at first?
facilitatorNotes: She keeps watching Roo and preparing to go home; apparent listening does not mean she has stopped caring for him.
evidence: but she still looked at Baby Roo.

questions.prompt: How is riding in Kanga’s pocket different from the flying Piglet had imagined?
facilitatorNotes: The jolts make him uncomfortable; the repeated up-and-down cries let the listener feel the bounces.
evidence: Ooooooo-ow, Ooooooo-ow, Ooooooo-ow

days.title: Kanga knows more than Piglet thinks — excerpt
days.challenge: Recognize when a character knowingly pretends.
days.focus: Compare a planned trick with a response that turns it around.
days.context: Piglet has taken Roo’s place in Kanga’s pocket. Kanga immediately recognizes him and knows Roo is safely with friends.
days.contentNote: Kanga imposes a bath and threatens medicine while teasing Piglet. This comic retaliation is not a model of respectful caregiving; an adult can acknowledge his discomfort.

excerpt.locator: Winnie-the-Pooh, Chapter VII; begins “Of course as soon as Kanga unbuttoned her pocket, …” and ends “… small and weak like Piglet, do you? Well, then!"”.

facilitatorNotes: The narrator says she sees what happened and decides to play a joke herself.
evidence: If they are having a joke with me, I will have a joke with them.

questions.prompt: Why does Piglet’s “Aha!” fail to work?
facilitatorNotes: He is alone without the others, and Kanga declines to respond as he expected.
evidence: But the others weren't there.

questions.prompt: What surprising change is happening to Rabbit while Piglet is having trouble?
facilitatorNotes: Rabbit is growing fond of Roo, undermining the original hostility to the newcomers.
evidence: feeling more fond of him every minute

days.title: New friends stay in the Forest — excerpt
days.challenge: Connect the final repeated schedule to a changed relationship.
days.focus: Distinguish the joking identity game from lasting inclusion.
days.context: Piglet is at Kanga’s house after the swap. Christopher Robin arrives, Roo is safe with Rabbit, and the friends’ foolish plan is nearing its end.
days.contentNote: The adults tease Piglet and give him medicine in this fantasy; discuss this as story behavior, not a way to treat children. The ending establishes friendship.

excerpt.locator: Winnie-the-Pooh, Chapter VII; begins “At that moment there was a knock at the …” and ends “… friend Christopher Robin. So they were all happy again.”.

questions.prompt: What has Christopher Robin seen that proves Piglet is not Roo?
facilitatorNotes: He has just seen the actual Roo playing at Rabbit’s house.
evidence: I've just seen Roo playing in Rabbit's house.

questions.prompt: Why does Piglet roll the last part of the way home?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to recover his familiar dirty color after the bath. The joke depends on color change rather than actual identity change.
evidence: to get his own nice comfortable colour again

questions.prompt: What does the final Tuesday routine tell us about the attempted exclusion?
facilitatorNotes: It has failed: Kanga and Roo stay, and visits become friendships.
evidence: So Kanga and Roo stayed in the Forest.

days.title: The Milkmaid and Her Pail
days.challenge: Remember a chain of imagined purchases while tracking one real object.
days.focus: An imagined gesture interrupts the very plan that caused it.
days.context: A dimity frock is a dress made of a light cotton fabric, and a chip hat is woven from thin strips. The story reflects historical clothing and courting customs.

facilitatorNotes: She imagines tossing her head and then actually tosses it, spilling the pail.

days.title: The Fairy-Land of Science — water held still and set free
days.challenge: Separate an observable change in water from the fairy-tale language used to describe it.
days.focus: A science lecturer borrows enchantment and rescue images to make freezing and thawing vivid.
days.context: From Lecture I of an 1888 science book. Buckley has compared Sleeping Beauty’s enchanted stillness with freezing water. Her frost-giant and rescuing sun are figurative language around a real observable change.
days.contentNote: This is historical science writing. Read its fairy figures as comparisons, not as the causes of weather.

questions.prompt: Which different places does the writer ask us to look for frozen water?
facilitatorNotes: Brook, pond, roof, trees, fountain, or window. Ask for two and the shape described at each.
evidence: transparent icicles

questions.prompt: Is the frost-giant a literal scientific cause in this passage?
facilitatorNotes: No; it personifies freezing. The measurable change is moving water becoming still ice.
evidence: the enchantments of the frost-giant

questions.prompt: What happens when warmth returns, and how does the writer make it sound like a rescue?
facilitatorNotes: Ice melts, drops fall, and the brook flows again; kisses and being set free make the sun resemble a fairy-tale rescuer.
evidence: it will be set free

days.title: Why the Wren Flies Close to the Earth
days.challenge: Notice a gap between the contest’s words and its intended meaning.
days.focus: A small bird finds a clever shortcut, and the other birds debate whether it is fair.
days.context: The birds decide to choose a ruler by a flying contest. Listen for a disagreement about what counts as flying highest.
days.contentNote: This is Holbrook’s 1902 literary adaptation, with imagined causes for natural features; it is not a scientific explanation or an authoritative account of a whole culture.

excerpt.locator: Why the Wren Flies Close to the Earth; begins “One day when the birds were all together, one …” and ends “… earth, and never tries to do what she cannot.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the first bird want a king? Is that a strong reason?
facilitatorNotes: The bird copies people and admits not knowing another reason. Invite the child to consider whether copying alone answers why a ruler is needed.
evidence: Oh, I do not know, but men have one.

questions.prompt: How does the wren get higher than the eagle without making the whole flight herself?
facilitatorNotes: She hides in the eagle’s feathers and flies upward only after it reaches its highest point.
evidence: the wren flew up from his back still higher

questions.prompt: Do you agree with the owl’s decision? What detail could support either side?
facilitatorNotes: Accept eagle because it carried both, or a question about the rule because the wren did reach higher. Explain that the owl’s “did not fly at all” ignores her last short flight.
evidence: The eagle is king, for he not only flew highest, but carried the wren on his back.

days.title: The Fairy-Land of Science — a question at the window
days.challenge: Compare a spoken explanation with an observation that helps a child remember.
days.focus: A small personal example supports the lecturer’s argument for investigating questions.
days.context: From Lecture I, where Buckley argues that careful observation can make an explanation memorable. Condensed means water vapor changing into liquid drops on a cooler surface.
days.contentNote: The historical passage mentions holding a cloth near a fire. Discuss that example as read; use the harmless window observation rather than heat or flame. The quoted child is learning English; her phrasing is reported affectionately, not for ridicule.

excerpt.locator: The Fairy-Land of Science — a question at the window; begins 'Mind, I do not advise you to be constantly asking questions of other people; for often a question qu'; ends 'n this little child some real picture in her mind of invisible water coming from her mouth, and making drops upon the window-pane?'. Source block range 46–47 in the documented transcription extraction.

questions.prompt: Why might an answer such as the sun dries it leave a question unfinished?
facilitatorNotes: A listener can repeat the words without picturing what happens. Buckley wants an observation that gives the words meaning.
evidence: rest satisfied with the sound of the words

questions.prompt: What does the aunt actually do after the child asks about rain indoors?
facilitatorNotes: She wipes the glass and breathes on it until new drops appear. Retell the demonstration before explaining it.
evidence: breathed on it several times

questions.prompt: What later detail suggests the child remembers the explanation?
facilitatorNotes: On a journey she follows drops on a window and says that she and her aunt made them. Her words connect new drops to the earlier observation.
evidence: Cissy and auntie made you.

days.title: Danny asks about his tail — excerpt
days.challenge: Notice a contrast between a cheerful setting and one character’s mood.
days.focus: Read an unhappy comparison alongside a neighbor’s patient attention.
days.context: Danny is unhappy about his short tail. Old Mr. Toad sends him to Grandfather Frog, who knows an old story about it; the story follows on the next two nights.
days.contentNote: Danny is ashamed of a body difference, and the narrator uses historical judgments about appearance.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter I; begins “Danny Meadow Mouse sat in his doorway and looked …” and ends “… as fast as his short legs would take him.”.

questions.prompt: What seems happy around Danny even though he is not?
facilitatorNotes: The sun plays behind clouds, birds sing, and the Breezes play. These details sharpen the contrast with Danny’s private worry.
evidence: the world was happy—all but Danny Meadow Mouse.

questions.prompt: How does Mr. Toad respond to Danny’s grumpy greeting?
facilitatorNotes: He continues kindly and asks after Danny’s health instead of matching the crossness.
evidence: just as if he hadn't noticed

questions.prompt: What shows Danny is eager but has not entirely forgotten courtesy?
facilitatorNotes: He hurries off but still calls thank you; he also brings an extra fly as a gift.
evidence: he caught one more for good measure

days.title: Grandfather Frog’s tale begins — excerpt
days.challenge: Keep track of what a character knows and what he only thinks he knows.
days.focus: A story inside the story begins, and a small clue—an acorn—shows the listener more than Mr. Meadow Mouse understands.
days.context: Danny has hurried to the Smiling Pool to ask Grandfather Frog why his tail is short. Grandfather Frog begins an old “why” story about Danny’s great-great-grandfather. To tote is to carry; a granary is a store of grain.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter I, Danny Meadow Mouse Learns Why His Tail Is Short; begins “When finally he reached the edge of the Smiling …” and ends “… one had been there and stolen all his acorns!”.

questions.prompt: What does Danny bring Grandfather Frog, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Four fat, foolish, green flies. Grandfather Frog knows Danny must want something; the flies are a gift that asks for the story.
evidence: I've brought you four fat, foolish, green flies.

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Meadow Mouse agree to carry Mr. Wharf Rat’s heavy bag?
facilitatorNotes: He feels flattered by a cousin he admires and is an obliging fellow. He does not know what is inside.
evidence: Now Mr. Meadow Mouse felt very much flattered

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Meadow Mouse say the bag holds potatoes?
facilitatorNotes: He does not know what is in it and is too proud to admit he is carrying it for someone else. His small untruth causes trouble later.
evidence: he didn't like to admit that he was working for another

questions.prompt: What clue makes Striped Chipmunk suspicious?
facilitatorNotes: Something drops from a hole in the bag, and it is an acorn, not a potato. He then finds his own acorns stolen.
evidence: It was a fat acorn.

days.title: Why the Meadow Mice have short tails — excerpt
days.challenge: Explain why a character stays silent and judge the result.
days.focus: A trial scene turns on loyalty and silence; the ending lets the Breezes answer Danny’s worry kindly.
days.context: Mr. Meadow Mouse has carried a bag of stolen acorns for his cousin, Mr. Wharf Rat, without knowing it. The meadow people find him asleep beside the bag.
days.contentNote: Old Mother Nature punishes the thief and shortens Mr. Meadow Mouse’s tail. The tale calls wharf rats outcasts who live on filth and garbage. It is a made-up “why” story, not natural history.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter I, to the chapter end; begins “"Then Striped Chipmunk ran to the house of his …” and ends “… that he had wished that his tail was long.”.

questions.prompt: Why won’t Mr. Meadow Mouse say where he got the bag of acorns?
facilitatorNotes: He has guessed his cousin is the thief, but he admires him and will not tell the world. Ask whether keeping quiet helps anyone.
evidence: He couldn't tell the world that Mr. Wharf Rat was a thief.

questions.prompt: What lesson does old Mother Nature give Mr. Meadow Mouse?
facilitatorNotes: Being loyal and not telling tales is good, but shielding someone who does wrong helps them keep doing wrong. Children may agree, disagree, or feel the punishment is too hard; ask for reasons.
evidence: it is also a very, very wrong thing to shield those who have done wrong

questions.prompt: How do the Merry Little Breezes answer Danny at the end?
facilitatorNotes: They say his short tail is not his fault and they love him just the same. Ask whether a tail can decide what someone is worth.
evidence: But it isn't your fault at all, Danny Meadow Mouse,

days.title: Breezes gather for a story — excerpt
days.challenge: Listen for repeated actions that communicate a request without stating it directly.
days.focus: Notice care for small neighbors during a storytelling ritual.
days.context: The tired Breezes rest at the pool and wonder about Peter Rabbit’s ears. Grandfather Frog’s explanation follows on the next night.
days.contentNote: This personified nature scene is fantasy.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter III; begins “The Merry Little Breezes of Old Mother West Wind …” and ends “… stopping to give Mrs. Redwing's cradle a gentle push.”.

questions.prompt: What job is Mother West Wind trying to finish while the Breezes rest?
facilitatorNotes: She is seeking a wandering raincloud to water thirsty plants.
evidence: before it had watered the thirsty little plants

questions.prompt: What gentle action do the Breezes repeat for Mrs. Redwing’s babies?
facilitatorNotes: They rock the nest, called a cradle, and give it another push while returning with flies.
evidence: each stopping to give Mrs. Redwing's cradle a gentle push.

questions.prompt: What does Grandfather Frog really want when he says four flies might help his memory?
facilitatorNotes: He is asking for food before telling the story; his throat-clearing delays the answer until they notice.
evidence: it is just possible that I might remember

days.title: Why Peter Rabbit’s ears are long — excerpt
days.challenge: Connect each change in a character’s body to the reason the story gives for it.
days.focus: A “why” story explains long ears and long legs as the results of curiosity and gossip.
days.context: The Merry Little Breezes have brought Grandfather Frog flies so that he will tell why Peter Rabbit’s ears are long. A prevaricator is someone who tells things that are not true; shiftless means lazy and careless.
days.contentNote: Old Mother Nature and Mr. North Wind pull Mr. Rabbit’s ears and hind legs long as a punishment in this made-up story.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter III, Why Peter Rabbit’s Ears Are Long, to the chapter end; begins “When Grandfather Frog had swallowed all the fat, foolish, …” and ends “… the wandering raincloud, which she had found at last.”.

questions.prompt: What bad habit did Mr. Rabbit have long ago?
facilitatorNotes: Curiosity: he listened to other people’s talk, even tiptoeing up to windows. Ask for one example from the story.
evidence: tiptoeing softly up to the windows to listen

questions.prompt: What happened on the Green Meadows because of Mr. Rabbit’s gossip?
facilitatorNotes: Neighbors quarrelled and turned their backs on each other because he told stories that were not true.
evidence: All because Mr. Rabbit had told so many stories that were not true.

questions.prompt: Why are Mr. Rabbit’s ears made long?
facilitatorNotes: So everyone who sees him will know it is not safe to talk near him. Children may also explain the long legs or the hole in the ground.
evidence: your ears shall be made long, that every one who sees you may know that it is not safe to talk when you are near

questions.prompt: Does old Mother Nature stop caring about Mr. Rabbit when she punishes him? How can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: No: the story says she loved him and was sorry for him, and that he was not altogether bad. Children may still think the punishment was harsh.
evidence: down in her heart she loved Mr. Rabbit

days.title: Too busy to tell — excerpt
days.challenge: Use a changing physical description to infer an unseen action.
days.focus: Connect a repeated refrain with a character’s immediate task.
days.context: It is nut-gathering season, and the Breezes want Striped Chipmunk to stop working and play.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter V; begins “It was one of Striped Chipmunk's busy days. Every …” and ends “… giggling, so that presently he had to smile too.”.

questions.prompt: What do the nut and frost details tell us about the season’s work?
facilitatorNotes: Ripe nuts are falling and opening, so Chipmunk is collecting food while it is available.
evidence: the sweet acorns are ripe

questions.prompt: Why is his head suddenly larger, and then normal again?
facilitatorNotes: He fills his cheek pouches with nuts and empties them at his store; the Breezes first jokingly mistake the bulge for mumps.
evidence: he filled his pockets with the brown nuts

questions.prompt: How do the Breezes help even after they decide he will not play?
facilitatorNotes: They shake nuts down for him before asking Grandfather Frog their question.
evidence: sent a shower of brown nuts rattling down to Striped Chipmunk

days.title: Small worker, difficult task — excerpt
days.challenge: Compare effort with results rather than counting the result alone.
days.focus: Notice unfair advantages and a character’s chosen response.
days.context: Grandfather Frog tells a fantasy about an ancestor of Chipmunk, long before the current animals’ time. Every squirrel must store a thousand nuts.
days.contentNote: Larger squirrels push Chipmunk and steal from him. The next scene recognizes his effort and repairs the loss; enduring bullying is not the lesson.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter V; begins “"Yes," said he, "it was when the world was …” and ends “… go up and shake them down for Mr. Chipmunk.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Chipmunk not envy the larger squirrels’ tails at first?
facilitatorNotes: He values his own striped coat and is content with it.
evidence: he had himself a beautiful striped coat

questions.prompt: Which obstacles make the same thousand-nut task harder for him?
facilitatorNotes: He is small, climbs poorly, has farther to carry nuts, and is pushed aside by larger cousins. Accept any two supported obstacles.
evidence: he had to be content with those on the ground

questions.prompt: What does he refuse to do even when nuts are difficult to find?
facilitatorNotes: He will not take a cousin’s dropped nut because he still regards it as the cousin’s.
evidence: if my cousin drops a nut, it is his nut just the same.

days.title: A reward for effort — excerpt
days.challenge: Use the judge’s actions to infer what she values.
days.focus: Distinguish a fantasy origin tale from an animal fact explanation.
days.context: Chipmunk has worked hard but has fewer nuts than the larger squirrels, and some of his store has been stolen. Mother Nature comes to inspect.
days.contentNote: The crowd calls the thief names; distinguish holding someone responsible from public humiliation. The magical origin of cheek pouches is fiction, not evolution.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter V; begins “"And then old Mother Nature came down across the …” and ends “… to shake down some more nuts for Striped Chipmunk.”.

questions.prompt: What does Chipmunk say instead of inventing an excuse for his smaller store?
facilitatorNotes: He says he has done his best; the trembling detail also shows exhaustion.
evidence: I've done the best I could

questions.prompt: How does Mother Nature repair the unfair distribution of nuts?
facilitatorNotes: She requires contributions from the others, more from the thief, and puts the collected nuts in Chipmunk’s store.
evidence: put them in the secret store-house of Mr. Chipmunk

questions.prompt: Why do cheek pockets make a fitting reward within this imaginary tale?
facilitatorNotes: They let the small worker carry more at once, reducing the very difficulty he faced.
evidence: that you may not have to work so hard

days.title: How the Blossoms Came to the Heather
days.challenge: Track how belonging changes before and after an outward reward.
days.focus: The mountain values the heather even before she has flowers.
days.context: Other plants have chosen places to live, but the shy heather still wants someone to welcome her.
days.contentNote: This is Holbrook’s 1902 literary adaptation, with imagined causes for natural features; it is not a scientific explanation or an authoritative account of a whole culture.

excerpt.locator: How the Blossoms Came to the Heather; begins “Only a little while after the earth was made, …” and ends “… blossoms she has had from that day to this.”.

questions.prompt: What can the heather offer the mountain even without blossoms?
facilitatorNotes: Her greenery can cover the rock and help shield it from wind and sunshine. She offers what she already has.
evidence: I will try to keep the wind and the sun away from you.

questions.prompt: When does the mountain first call the heather beautiful—before or after her blossoms appear?
facilitatorNotes: Before. The mountain praises her bright green covering, showing that its welcome does not depend on flowers.
evidence: See how beautiful my little heather is!

questions.prompt: How does the ending answer the heather’s earlier wish?
facilitatorNotes: She wanted someone glad to see her; the mountain’s welcome already answers that, and the later flowers add a reward.
evidence: I wish there was some one who would be glad to see me

days.title: How Flax Was Given to Men
days.challenge: Keep track of speech within speech and a changed opinion.
days.focus: A useful plant becomes more valuable to the family than dazzling jewels.
days.context: A hunter returns with a gift from the goddess Holda. His wife first thinks he has chosen badly.
days.contentNote: This is Holbrook’s 1902 literary adaptation, with imagined causes for natural features; it is not a scientific explanation or an authoritative account of a whole culture. Holda is a figure in this myth, not a documented historical teacher of the first weavers.

excerpt.locator: How Flax Was Given to Men; begins “"You have been on the mountain a long time," …” and ends “… all the diamonds in the hall of the goddess."”.

questions.prompt: Which gift does the hunter choose instead of jewels? What draws him to it?
facilitatorNotes: He chooses the blue flower in Holda’s hand; her presence turns his thoughts away from precious stones. Let the child notice beauty and personal meaning.
evidence: the little blue flower in your lily-white hand

questions.prompt: Why is the gift more than a single flower that will fade?
facilitatorNotes: Holda includes seed and promises instruction; the family can grow more and learn to make linen.
evidence: She gave me the flower and the seed of it

questions.prompt: What makes the wife reverse her first judgment?
facilitatorNotes: Seeing the finished linen and learning its usefulness changes what she values. Compare her first complaint with her final preference.
evidence: the linen is fairer than the pearls

days.title: The Fairy-Land of Science — morning light in a room
days.challenge: Order observations from faint outlines to detailed color, then connect them with a model.
days.focus: A familiar awakening leads to an explanation using a turning globe.
days.context: From the opening of Lecture II, before the book’s later and now-obsolete account of light in ether. This excerpt connects dawn with Earth’s rotation. England is the lecturer’s example location, not the only place where this happens.
days.contentNote: If demonstrating the model, an adult can use a cool flashlight and a ball. The historical lamp wording does not require flame.

excerpt.locator: The Fairy-Land of Science — morning light in a room; begins 'Did you ever wake quite early in the morning, when it was pitch-dark and you could see nothing, not '; ends ' lay in bed and saw the light appear; and we have to learn to-day what those beams are which fall upon us and what they do for us.'. Source block range 74–76 in the documented transcription extraction.

questions.prompt: What can the watcher distinguish before all the small details appear?
facilitatorNotes: Dim furniture outlines first, then light cloth versus dark wardrobe. Track the stages rather than naming only daylight.
evidence: dim outline of the furniture

questions.prompt: What movement explains sunrise for this particular place?
facilitatorNotes: Earth turns, bringing the place toward sunlight. The writer distinguishes the usual expression rising from the model’s explanation.
evidence: our earth has been turning slowly round

questions.prompt: What do the lamp and the marked spot represent?
facilitatorNotes: Lamp is Sun; marked spot is a place on Earth. Ask what must turn in this model and what the observation is meant to explain.
evidence: let a lighted lamp represent the sun

days.title: The Story of the Earth and the Sky
days.challenge: Hold an imagined possibility beside the characters’ familiar experience.
days.focus: A dream challenges “there is only just here,” and both parents eventually see new beauty.
days.context: Earth and Sky begin close together in this personified origin tale. Their son imagines a world with room for light.
days.contentNote: This is Holbrook’s 1902 literary adaptation, with imagined causes for natural features; it is not a scientific explanation or an authoritative account of a whole culture. Sky complains of discomfort when resting on mountain peaks; the scene is personified fantasy, not an account of the atmosphere.

excerpt.locator: The Story of the Earth and the Sky; begins “The sky used to be very close to the …” and ends “… good-morning message from the beautiful earth to the sky.”.

questions.prompt: Why do Earth and Sky doubt the Shining One’s dream at first?
facilitatorNotes: They have never known another arrangement; Sky even denies that a higher place exists. Their experience limits what they imagine.
evidence: There is only just here.

questions.prompt: Why does Sky ask for two cloaks instead of being content with one?
facilitatorNotes: The starry dark-blue cloak suits night, but he wants a lighter daytime covering. The image gives the visible sky two costumes.
evidence: Give me another cloak for the day.

questions.prompt: How do Earth and Sky send messages when they are far apart?
facilitatorNotes: Sky sends gentle rain and Earth sends a rising cloud. Ask how these images turn weather into affection.
evidence: It is carrying a good-morning message from the beautiful earth to the sky.

days.title: Why All Men Love the Moon
days.challenge: Compare three parallel responses and notice the smallest character’s different choice.
days.focus: The tale contrasts keeping pleasures for oneself with remembering someone absent.
days.context: Thunder and Lightning give a feast to three children of the Star Mother: Sun, Wind and Moon.
days.contentNote: This is Holbrook’s 1902 literary adaptation, with imagined causes for natural features; it is not a scientific explanation or an authoritative account of a whole culture. The mother assigns magical consequences to selfishness. The title’s “all men” is the author’s generalising language, not a claim that everyone has the same feelings about the moon.

excerpt.locator: Why All Men Love the Moon; begins “Thunder and Lightning were going to give a feast. …” and ends “… sun and the wind, but never from the moon.”.

questions.prompt: Which creatures help prepare the feast without bringing food?
facilitatorNotes: Butterflies and hummingbirds arrange flowers; colourful birds help decorate, and waters supply music. Different gifts contribute to one celebration.
evidence: the waves and the brooks agreed to make their most charming music

questions.prompt: What do Sun’s and Wind’s answers reveal about what happened to their gifts?
facilitatorNotes: Sun keeps his food for himself; Wind eats his because carrying it is tiring. Neither saves something for the waiting mother.
evidence: I brought only what I am going to eat myself

questions.prompt: What is unusual about the Moon’s gift beyond food?
facilitatorNotes: She brings colour and even music, impossible physical gifts that make her generosity expansive in the story.
evidence: there was even some of the charming music

days.title: Games by the pool — excerpt
days.challenge: Match different actions with different characters’ abilities.
days.focus: Listen for someone who stays outside the shared celebration.
days.context: The meadow animals gather for friendly demonstrations of jumping, climbing, and swimming.
days.contentNote: The narrator repeatedly describes Johnny’s round body. Focus on his good spirits and different abilities, not judging people by body size.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter VI; begins “Johnny Chuck waddled down the Lone Little Path across …” and ends “And everybody shouted "Hurrah!" Everybody but Reddy Fox.”.

questions.prompt: How does Johnny respond when his own jump ends in a tumble?
facilitatorNotes: He laughs loudest himself, so the scene presents shared fun rather than his being devastated by failure.
evidence: Johnny Chuck laughed loudest of all.

questions.prompt: Which three abilities receive separate celebrations?
facilitatorNotes: Peter’s jumping, Happy Jack’s climbing, and Little Joe’s swimming; each animal shines in a different way.
evidence: I can swim faster than anybody here

questions.prompt: Whose name keeps appearing after “everybody but,” and what pattern does that build?
facilitatorNotes: Reddy Fox; he does not join the praise for others, suggesting he wants admiration for himself.
evidence: Everybody but Reddy Fox.

days.title: A boast with a weak spot — excerpt
days.challenge: Listen for a claim that another character’s reaction disproves.
days.focus: Compare feeling inferior with trying to sound superior.
days.context: The animals have shown their skills. Johnny wonders what he can do well, while Reddy dislikes the attention given to others.
days.contentNote: The friends tease Reddy for boasting. Fear is not shameful; discuss why an exaggerated claim is unreliable rather than mocking fear.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter VI; begins “"What can you do, Jimmy Skunk?" asked Peter Rabbit, …” and ends “… can run so fast, you can't even catch me."”.

questions.prompt: How does Jimmy’s perfume claim affect everyone without his using it?
facilitatorNotes: They hurry away because they know what skunk spray means; he kindly refrains.
evidence: But please don't!

questions.prompt: What quality does Johnny forget while comparing skills?
facilitatorNotes: He forgets that being sunny-hearted and good-natured is valued, even without winning a contest.
evidence: everybody loved him

questions.prompt: How does Reddy’s reaction to the hound’s name challenge his claim of fearlessness?
facilitatorNotes: He looks around nervously even though the hound is absent. A listener can compare the boast with his action.
evidence: nervously and anxiously looked over the Green Meadows

days.title: Johnny finds his skill — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow two opposite digging directions through a chase.
days.focus: Find the practical ability hidden by comparisons with others.
days.context: Angry Reddy lunges at Johnny beside an old burrow. This scene includes Johnny’s immediate safe escape.
days.contentNote: A fox chases Johnny, who escapes unharmed within the selection. Others laugh at the dusty fox; invite empathy without endorsing the chase or ridicule.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter VI; begins “Reddy Fox just glared at him for a minute, …” and ends “… knew that none could dig so fast as he.”.

questions.prompt: Why can Johnny enter the hole while Reddy cannot simply follow?
facilitatorNotes: It is too small for Reddy, who must enlarge it.
evidence: the hole was too small for Reddy Fox to enter

questions.prompt: What different direction does Johnny choose that makes his escape possible?
facilitatorNotes: He digs upward toward the surface while Reddy digs into the tunnel after him.
evidence: instead of digging down he dug up

questions.prompt: Why is Johnny’s earlier discontent gone at the end?
facilitatorNotes: He realizes he can dig exceptionally well; the chase reveals a strength the earlier contests did not test.
evidence: none could dig so fast as he.

days.title: The Fairy-Land of Science — fans inside the hive
days.challenge: Follow an explanation linking a crowded place, a problem, and a visible movement.
days.focus: The lecturer interprets wing movements as a way of moving air.
days.context: One complete explanatory paragraph from Lecture IX about work in a honeybee hive. It follows an account of the colony preparing for winter. Ventilate means move fresh air through a space.
days.contentNote: This is Buckley’s historical description of honeybee fanning, not a claim that every hive always arranges its bees exactly this way. Observe insects from a comfortable distance without touching a hive.

excerpt.locator: The Fairy-Land of Science — fans inside the hive; begins 'Although the hive has now become comparatively quiet and the work goes on without excitement, yet ev'; ends 's, this time with their backs towards the entrance, and fan in the same manner, and in this way air is sent into all the passages.'. questions.prompt: What problem does the writer identify inside a crowded hive?
facilitatorNotes: Many insects together make it warm, and the air needs circulation.
evidence: the heat will become very great

questions.prompt: Why does the explanation mention windows?
facilitatorNotes: It compares a hive with a house: bees cannot open windows, so they move air at the entrance.
evidence: no windows that they can open

questions.prompt: Which action would an observer look for to investigate the writer’s claim?
facilitatorNotes: Bees moving their wings near the entrance. Distinguish seeing wing movement from inferring the airflow and its purpose.
evidence: they wave them to and fro

days.title: The Fairy-Land of Science — watching a bee’s flower visits
days.challenge: Distinguish what a watcher sees from the human motives the writer imagines.
days.focus: A quiet garden scene narrows to a question about a bee’s repeated choice of flower.
days.context: The opening garden scene of Lecture X, Bees and Flowers. Buckley calls the sweet liquid in flowers honey; the liquid bees collect is nectar, which they later process into honey. Watch safely from a distance.

questions.prompt: How does the leisurely humble-bee differ from the hive-bee in this account?
facilitatorNotes: One stays longer in larkspurs; the other moves quickly among blossoms. Humble-bee is an older name for bumblebee.
evidence: moves busily and quickly

questions.prompt: What pattern does the writer invite us to follow on one trip?
facilitatorNotes: The hive-bee keeps visiting the same kind of flower before going home.
evidence: keeps to one

questions.prompt: Can looking at the bee prove it feels happy or speaks No honey there?
facilitatorNotes: No; those phrases are the author’s imaginative reading of visible behavior. We can observe where it goes and how long it stays.
evidence: as if to say

days.title: A bush waits for its season — excerpt
days.challenge: Track a change across spring, summer, and autumn.
days.focus: Notice how a different timetable first looks like failure.
days.context: A little bush grows beside the brook among bushes that flower in spring. This story personifies the plants’ feelings.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter XI; begins “Way down beside the Laughing Brook grew a little …” and ends “… stopped to look at it and to praise it.”.

questions.prompt: Why does growing green leaves not make this bush feel included at first?
facilitatorNotes: The others also produce buds and flowers, which it lacks; it compares itself with their next stage.
evidence: no little brown buds appeared

questions.prompt: What does it keep doing while disappointed?
facilitatorNotes: It continues to grow, making leaves larger despite its feelings.
evidence: it bravely kept on growing and growing and growing.

questions.prompt: What reversal happens after the other bushes lose their leaves?
facilitatorNotes: Its buds open into yellow flowers, making it the only flowering bush then.
evidence: it was the only bush which had any flowers.

days.title: Little packages and new plants — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow seeds through more than one seasonal cycle.
days.focus: Notice the story’s images for waiting, protection, and new life.
days.context: The late-flowering bush has found its season. After its yellow flowers fall, small packages remain. The chapter ends by telling the bush’s name.
days.contentNote: The fox briefly mistakes popping seed cases for shooting; no weapon is present. The ending describes witch hazel lotion from the medicine closet as a 1911 household remedy for bumps.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter XI; begins “Colder grew the weather and colder. Johnny Chuck tucked …” and ends “… to make them feel better when they are hurt.”.

questions.prompt: What stays on the bush through winter after the flowers are gone?
facilitatorNotes: Small packages, one for each flower, later developing into nutlike seed cases.
evidence: tiny little packages, one for every little flower

questions.prompt: How do the seeds leave their cases, and which sounds help us hear it?
facilitatorNotes: The cases burst with popping and snapping; read the sound words aloud together.
evidence: Pop! pop! snap! snap! hippetty hop!

questions.prompt: Why is the bush less lonely when the next seedlings appear?
facilitatorNotes: They will grow into plants like itself; its different season now promises continuity rather than isolation.
evidence: it knew that it would no longer be lonely.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the little bush, and what gift does the storyteller say it gives people?
facilitatorNotes: Witch hazel. The storyteller says a lotion made from it is poured on bumps to make them feel better; that is how families used it in 1911.
evidence: Why, it is the witch hazel.

days.title: Finding something useful to do — excerpt
days.challenge: Notice a repeated invitation whose answer changes the characters’ goal.
days.focus: Read helping as an alternative when companions are busy.
days.context: The Breezes want playmates, but every animal they meet needs to find food or attend to work.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter XIII; begins “Old Mother West Wind came down from the Purple …” and ends “… Peter Rabbit, and straightway began to eat his breakfast.”.

questions.prompt: Why do Peter, Jimmy, and Billy give the same “Can’t” answer for different reasons?
facilitatorNotes: Each has a different breakfast task; the repeated refusal reveals a busy world rather than dislike of the Breezes.
evidence: I have to catch a trout for Grandfather Mink's breakfast

questions.prompt: What idea turns the lack of work of their own into a purpose?
facilitatorNotes: They decide to help someone else rather than keep asking others to stop.
evidence: let's do something for somebody else!

questions.prompt: How does a Breeze guide Peter without carrying the carrots?
facilitatorNotes: It brings their smell to his nose and leads him to the field.
evidence: taking the smell of them with him to tickle the nose of Peter Rabbit

days.title: Breakfast beneath a stone — excerpt
days.challenge: Infer how hunger affects a character’s response.
days.focus: Notice that useful help goes beyond trying to change a mood.
days.context: One Breeze has helped Peter find carrots. Another finds a clue that may help hungry Jimmy Skunk.
days.contentNote: The Breeze first ruffles Jimmy’s coat despite his irritation. A listener may reasonably think it should offer help sooner rather than teasing him.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter XIII; begins “Another Merry Little Breeze, slipping up the Crooked Little …” and ends “… as he started to catch beetles for his breakfast.”.

questions.prompt: Which visible clue tells the Breeze that Jimmy might find food here?
facilitatorNotes: Beetle legs protrude from under a stone.
evidence: the hind legs of a fat beetle sticking out from under a flat stone

questions.prompt: Why is Jimmy especially cross before the Breeze speaks?
facilitatorNotes: He has looked without finding breakfast. His hunger explains his mood without making rude words kind.
evidence: he hadn't had any breakfast

questions.prompt: What turns the Breeze’s visit into practical help rather than just teasing?
facilitatorNotes: It leads him to the beetles and he can eat; the thank-you follows the discovery.
evidence: started to catch beetles for his breakfast.

days.title: Bags of flower gold — excerpt
days.challenge: Use the story’s metaphor without taking it literally.
days.focus: Hear a repeated refusal turn into a sign of purposeful activity.
days.context: The other Breezes find the bee carrying a special kind of “gold” between flowers. The final scene will name it pollen.
days.contentNote: Flower “gold” is a fantasy picture of pollen; the scene is not a precise account of bee behavior or how every plant is pollinated.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter XIII; begins “And the Little Breeze laughed happily as he danced …” and ends “… we are busy, busy, busy," and they laughed happily.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Bumble say he must carry something as well as gather honey?
facilitatorNotes: Mother Nature has required an exchange between flowers. In the fantasy, receiving depends on carrying.
evidence: carry a sack of gold from each flower I visit to the next flower I visit

questions.prompt: How do the Breezes combine work with the movement they already enjoy?
facilitatorNotes: They dance from flower to flower and race across gaps, so useful activity still feels playful.
evidence: Yet after all it was a kind of play

questions.prompt: How has the meaning of “Can’t” changed when Peter asks them to play?
facilitatorNotes: Now the Breezes have their own helpful work; the repeated word reverses the opening situation.
evidence: we have work to do!

days.title: No tiny flower overlooked — excerpt
days.challenge: Connect a metaphor to the real word revealed at the end.
days.focus: Notice an ending that turns one day’s activity into an imagined continuing role.
days.context: The Breezes have spent the day helping animals and carrying flower “gold.” Mother Nature sees their work.
days.contentNote: The narrator personifies wind and pollen and calls several animals lazy. Treat the imagined jobs as literary characters, not scientific judgments about animals.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter XIII; begins “When they reached the Laughing Brook they found Billy …” and ends “… Meadows. And this is the happiest time of all.”.

questions.prompt: What does the statement about the tiniest flower show about their attention?
facilitatorNotes: They include even small, easy-to-miss flowers rather than only the largest ones.
evidence: No wee flower was too tiny

questions.prompt: What lasting job does Mother Nature give them?
facilitatorNotes: They are to distribute the flowers’ gold, turning a voluntary day’s help into a continuing task.
evidence: should have charge of the distribution of the gold of the flowers

questions.prompt: Which final word explains what the story has been calling gold?
facilitatorNotes: Pollen; ask the child to revisit the bag-of-gold image with that word in mind.
evidence: call pollen

days.title: Saint Cuthbert’s Peace — Part 1: The Shepherd Boy
days.challenge: Follow how a person’s early life prepares him for later choices.
days.focus: Cuthbert’s outdoor boyhood, his vision and his kindness explain why he later chooses a life among the birds.
days.context: Abbie Farwell Brown retold this saint legend for children in 1900. Cuthbert was a shepherd boy in Scotland more than a thousand years ago. An abbey is a home for monks; a hermit lives alone.

excerpt.locator: Saint Cuthbert’s Peace, from the opening; begins “SAINT CUTHBERT was a Scotch shepherd boy who tended …” and ends “… wild outdoor life with the birds whom he loved.”.

questions.prompt: What was Cuthbert like as a shepherd boy?
facilitatorNotes: Strong, fast and good at games, and he learned the ways of animals and loved the birds. Accept any detail from the opening.
evidence: Especially he loved the birds.

questions.prompt: What did Cuthbert see in the sky one night while he watched his sheep?
facilitatorNotes: A path of light with angels carrying a beautiful blossom, which he took to be a holy man’s soul. It led him to become a monk.
evidence: a band of angels came from heaven

questions.prompt: Which sea animals came to Cuthbert after his cold bath, and what did they do?
facilitatorNotes: Two brown otters licked his frozen feet and dried him with their fur. Ask why the story includes this.
evidence: two brown otters came up out of the sea

questions.prompt: Why did Cuthbert leave the Abbey to become a hermit?
facilitatorNotes: After twelve years indoors he longed for fresh air, the sky, and the birds he loved.
evidence: he longed to get out into the fresh air and under the sky once more

days.title: Saint Cuthbert’s Peace — Part 2: The Island Home
days.challenge: Hold practical details beside the narrator’s imaginative descriptions.
days.focus: A solitary home is shown as full of companionship.
days.context: Cuthbert has left the Abbey to live as a hermit on the rocky island of Farne, where birds visit him.
days.contentNote: The narrator presents some legendary details as fact; that voice is part of the original text, not historical verification.

excerpt.locator: Saint Cuthbert’s Peace — The Island Home; begins “He built his nest on a wild little island …” and ends “… his shoes with, and it lasted a long time.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator call Cuthbert’s home a “nest,” even though he is human?
facilitatorNotes: It is a small shelter among birds, built from simple materials; the comparison connects his way of living with theirs.
evidence: The nest was really a hole in the ground

questions.prompt: Why are the birds wrong to think that people cannot reach the island?
facilitatorNotes: They remember that people have no wings but forget about boats; the narrator calls boats “with wings.”
evidence: though men cannot fly they make boats with wings

questions.prompt: How does the narrator distinguish the gift of suet from the grander story people tell?
facilitatorNotes: People say birds bring heavenly food; the narrator gives a smaller story about stolen barley and a compensating gift used on shoes. Still frame the whole as a legend.
evidence: He did not eat it, however, as they expected he would

days.title: Saint Cuthbert’s Peace — Part 3: The Promise
days.challenge: Explain what a promise means and judge the stories told to prove it.
days.focus: The legend’s title is explained: Cuthbert’s “Peace” protects his birds, and two stories claim to prove its power.
days.context: Cuthbert lives as a hermit on the island of Farne among the sea-birds. An eider-duck lines her nest with soft down from her breast. To bequeath is to leave something to others after you die.
days.contentNote: A servant kills and eats a protected eider-duck and is punished; a hawk eats a tame sparrow and is made to fly round the island. The narrator says later men killed many of the trusting birds.

excerpt.locator: Saint Cuthbert’s Peace, to the end; begins “Now Cuthbert loved all these birds dearly, especially the …” and ends “… the cruel hands which dare to hurt his birds.”.

questions.prompt: What is the promise called “Saint Cuthbert’s Peace”?
facilitatorNotes: No one should harm or kill the birds on the island without being punished, and the birds must not hurt each other.
evidence: He promised that no one should harm or kill them on that island

questions.prompt: How was Liveing’s secret found out?
facilitatorNotes: The sea washed a lump of the duck’s bones and feathers onto the chapel steps. The story says even the sea kept the promise.
evidence: he found a lump of bones and feathers rolled together

questions.prompt: What happened to the hawk that ate the sparrow, and who helped it?
facilitatorNotes: It had to fly around the island until Bartholomew took pity, caught it and sent it away. Ask whether the hermit was kind to the hawk.
evidence: Bartholomew caught the tired hawk by his wings

questions.prompt: The storyteller is “sure” that Saint Cuthbert still punishes people who hurt his birds. Is that something the story proves, or something the storyteller believes?
facilitatorNotes: It is the storyteller’s belief in the legend; children may say what they think and why. Also notice the sadness about birds that trusted people.
evidence: But I am sure that Saint Cuthbert's dreadful charm still binds the murderers.

days.title: Saint Gerasimus and the Lion — Part I: The Thorn
days.challenge: Revise an initial impression when new details appear.
days.focus: The frightening roar becomes a request for help.
days.context: Abbie Farwell Brown retold this saint legend for children in 1900. Gerasimus is walking beside the River Jordan with a donkey when he hears an unfamiliar sound. A monastery is a home for a religious community.
days.contentNote: A thorn hurts the lion’s paw and is removed without graphic detail. Fear is normal; the narrator’s claim that goodness makes someone fearless should not be treated as a rule.

excerpt.locator: Saint Gerasimus and the Lion — The Thorn; begins “ONE fine morning Saint Gerasimus was walking briskly along …” and ends “… say, "Thank you, kind man. I shall not forget."”.

questions.prompt: Which detail changes the roar from merely frightening to sad?
facilitatorNotes: Its whining and sobbing sound, followed by the lion’s limp, suggests pain rather than an attack.
evidence: a sort of whining growl ending in a sob

questions.prompt: How does the lion show where he needs help without using words?
facilitatorNotes: He holds up and shakes his right forepaw. The story invites reading gesture as communication.
evidence: he held up his right fore paw and shook it

questions.prompt: How does the ending of this scene answer the donkey’s fear?
facilitatorNotes: Instead of attacking, the lion lies still for help and licks the man’s hand afterward. Fear was understandable, though this legend gives an unusual outcome.
evidence: the lion licked Gerasimus' hand

days.title: Saint Gerasimus and the Lion — Part I: A Place by the Fire
days.challenge: Track contrasting reactions to the same visitor.
days.focus: Familiar pet images make the lion’s welcome seem both funny and tender.
days.context: Gerasimus has removed a painful thorn from a lion’s paw. The lion follows him toward the monastery rather than returning to the wild.
days.contentNote: The story jokes about monks’ body sizes and invents a plant-eating lion. Body size does not determine worth, and actual lions need species-appropriate diets.

excerpt.locator: Saint Gerasimus and the Lion — A Place by the Fire; begins “Now when the Saint had finished this good deed …” and ends “… to go back to the desert with its thorns.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Gerasimus let the lion follow even while he is uncertain about the monks’ reaction?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks sending away the still-limping animal would be unkind. His hesitation gives the unexpected companion a chance.
evidence: it did not seem polite or kind to drive him away

questions.prompt: What comparisons turn the lion into a familiar household creature?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator compares his exploring to a kitten and his sleeping pose to a big cat. Ask the listener to picture how these soften the frightening first impression.
evidence: just as a kitten does in its new home

questions.prompt: How does the lion show he values the friendship even though he dislikes supper?
facilitatorNotes: He eats the porridge and greens because Gerasimus wishes it and offers to share his own meal. This is the legend’s human-like lion, not real lion nutrition.
evidence: Share and share alike, brother.

days.title: Saint Gerasimus and the Lion — Part II: The Lost Donkey
days.challenge: Separate what really happened from what a character believes happened.
days.focus: A wrong guess turns the lion’s loyalty into a long, unfair punishment.
days.context: Leo the lion now lives at the monastery and helps the donkey fetch water. Gerasimus leaves Leo to watch the donkey while he talks with a man.
days.contentNote: Gerasimus wrongly blames Leo, strikes him with a switch, and the monks punish him with hard work; the mistake is set right in the next part.

excerpt.locator: Saint Gerasimus and the Lion, Part II; begins “WHEREVER Gerasimus went the lion went also. Best of …” and ends “… the world was against him, and truth was dead.”.

questions.prompt: What happens while Leo is supposed to be watching the donkey?
facilitatorNotes: He falls asleep; the donkey wanders off and a passing Camel Driver steals it. Ask the child to put the three events in order.
evidence: the next moment Leo was sound asleep

questions.prompt: Why does Gerasimus think Leo ate the donkey?
facilitatorNotes: Leo is roaring and foaming, the donkey is gone, and only the water-jar is left. The narrator calls it a great mistake, so the listener knows more than Gerasimus.
evidence: Then Gerasimus made a great mistake.

questions.prompt: Leo is the King of Beasts. Why does he let himself be harnessed like a donkey?
facilitatorNotes: He remembers how Gerasimus took out the thorn, so he accepts the work out of love and gratitude, even though it is unfair.
evidence: remembered how he had taken out that cruel thorn

questions.prompt: How does the story show that Leo is sad during his punishment?
facilitatorNotes: He grows thin, his mane is tangled, and he has white hairs in his whiskers; he hopes something will show it was a mistake.
evidence: He was growing thinner and thinner.

days.title: Saint Gerasimus and the Lion — Part II: The Truth Comes Out
days.challenge: Explain how one discovery changes how every character is treated.
days.focus: The lion proves the truth without words; the legend ends with a lifelong friendship and the narrator’s view of its ending.
days.context: Leo has been punished for a crime he did not commit. Gerasimus takes him to a town to carry home baskets of food.
days.contentNote: At the end Gerasimus dies in old age and Leo dies of grief on his grave; the narrator calls this “not a sad thing.”

excerpt.locator: Saint Gerasimus and the Lion, Part II, to the end; begins “It was a sad time for Gerasimus, too; for …” and ends “… could sleep together side by side in the garden.”.

questions.prompt: How does Leo show Gerasimus what really happened to the donkey?
facilitatorNotes: He growls at the Camel Driver and seizes the stolen donkey’s bridle, so Gerasimus begins to suspect the truth.
evidence: when he saw Leo seize the donkey's bridle, he began to suspect the truth

questions.prompt: What does Gerasimus say to Leo once he understands his mistake?
facilitatorNotes: He says he made Leo suffer cruelly for a crime he did not do, and promises to make it up to him. Ask how the monks then make it up to Leo.
evidence: I have made you suffer cruelly for a crime of which you were not guilty.

questions.prompt: The narrator says the ending “was not a sad thing.” Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator thinks it is beautiful that the friends were never parted. Children may feel it is sad, or both sad and beautiful; accept either with a reason from the words.
evidence: But this was not a sad thing that happened.

days.title: Saint Blaise and His Beasts — Part 1: The Forest Visitors
days.challenge: Notice how care is shown through waiting, listening and returning something.
days.focus: Kindness reaches both the animal who did wrong and the person harmed.
days.context: Abbie Farwell Brown retold this saint legend for children in 1900. Blaise lived in Sebaste, in Armenia, about 1,700 years ago; he studied medicine and cared for animals.
days.contentNote: A wolf carries away a pig, which is returned unharmed.

excerpt.locator: Saint Blaise and His Beasts — The Forest Visitors; begins “THIS is the story of a Saint who loved …” and ends “… a dish of fresh milk to cool his throat.”.

questions.prompt: How do the animals behave when they arrive during Blaise’s prayers?
facilitatorNotes: They wait patiently outside instead of interrupting; their care mirrors the care he gives them.
evidence: waited in a patient, wistful group at the door of his cave

questions.prompt: Why does Blaise remind the wolf that the pig is also his friend?
facilitatorNotes: He asks the wolf to recognise another creature’s value and the woman’s loss, not just its own desire.
evidence: the Pig was a friend of mine, too

questions.prompt: What details show that the problem is repaired rather than merely discussed?
facilitatorNotes: The wolf brings the pig home alive; the woman greets it joyfully, and the wolf then receives approval.
evidence: the Pig run grunting into her yard

days.title: Saint Blaise and His Beasts — Part 2: The Soldiers Come
days.challenge: Notice how the animals’ behaviour tells the story of Blaise’s danger.
days.focus: The legend contrasts the animals’ loyalty with the cruelty of the soldiers, and ends with how Blaise is remembered.
days.context: Blaise has become a bishop and lives in a forest cave where wild animals visit him. In his time the Roman emperor was having Christians put to death. An arena was a place where people watched fights with wild beasts.
days.contentNote: Blaise is imprisoned, tortured and beheaded for his faith, told in a few sentences without description; soldiers drown in a lake.

excerpt.locator: Saint Blaise and His Beasts, to the end; begins “Saint Blaise was chosen Bishop by the Christians who …” and ends “… their ancestors, the beasts in the forests of Armenia.”.

questions.prompt: Why can’t the soldiers find any wild beasts in the mountains?
facilitatorNotes: The animals are all at Blaise’s cave making their morning call. The soldiers find them sitting quietly around him.
evidence: there were the animals, all the fierce beasts whom they feared

questions.prompt: What kind thing does Blaise do on his way to prison?
facilitatorNotes: He cures a child who is choking on a bone. The story says this is why people once prayed to him for sore throats.
evidence: Saint Blaise touched the baby's throat and the trouble was gone.

questions.prompt: How do the forest animals act after Blaise is taken away?
facilitatorNotes: They howl and moan and search for him like stray dogs that have lost their master. Their sadness shows how much he meant to them.
evidence: went sniffing and searching for him everywhere, like stray dogs who have lost their master

questions.prompt: How does the storyteller say Blaise was remembered long afterward?
facilitatorNotes: People lit bonfires on hills on the third of February, and the storyteller imagines the animals remembering him too.
evidence: light great bonfires on all the hills

days.title: Saint Comgall and the Mice — Part 1: The Swans
days.challenge: Compare two approaches to the same animals.
days.focus: Quiet presence succeeds where busy coaxing does not.
days.context: Abbie Farwell Brown retold this saint legend for children in 1900. Comgall ran a monastery school at Bangor in Ireland. The storyteller promises the mice at the end; first comes a story about swans.
days.contentNote: The narrator’s joke that peanuts had not been “invented” is not a botanical fact. Do not try to hold or feed wild swans.

excerpt.locator: Saint Comgall and the Mice — The Swans Episode; begins “AT the place where the Irish Sea is narrowest …” and ends “… but loved him as soon as they saw him.”.

questions.prompt: How do the pupils try to attract the swans, and what is missing from their plan?
facilitatorNotes: They search for food in their pockets and whistle and call, but have no food to offer.
evidence: trying in every way to make the swans swim ashore

questions.prompt: How does Comgall’s approach sound different from the pupils’ efforts?
facilitatorNotes: He goes quietly and makes a small crooning sound rather than many calls. His manner matters in the legend.
evidence: Making a little croony sound in his throat

questions.prompt: Why are the pupils especially surprised when a swan sits in his lap?
facilitatorNotes: The swans have never met him either, so prior acquaintance cannot explain their different response; the narrator attributes it to love.
evidence: the swans were as truly strangers to Saint Comgall as to the rest of them

days.title: Saint Comgall and the Mice — Part 2: The Mice
days.challenge: Hear how a word with two meanings makes a prediction come true.
days.focus: Comgall’s warning, “The mouse shall have your grain,” is fulfilled in a way the Prince does not expect.
days.context: Comgall has made friends with swans. Now the storyteller tells the stranger story about his friends the mice. A famine is a time when there is not enough food; a goblet is a cup.
days.contentNote: The Prince would rather let people starve than share his grain, and the storyteller calls his old mother wicked and miserly; the mice eat all his grain.

excerpt.locator: Saint Comgall and the Mice, to the end; begins “But this next is the stranger story. Mice are …” and ends “… this way to punish a selfish and cruel man.”.

questions.prompt: Why are Comgall and his monks so hungry?
facilitatorNotes: There is a famine, and the Prince Croadh has full barns but will not give or even sell any grain.
evidence: But he was a selfish, stingy man and would not give away or even sell his stores

questions.prompt: What does Comgall offer the Prince, and how does the Prince answer?
facilitatorNotes: His silver goblet in exchange for grain; the Prince laughs and keeps his grain for his “old Mouse,” his mother.
evidence: You keep your silver goblet and I will keep my golden grain.

questions.prompt: Comgall says, “The mouse shall have your grain.” How does that come true?
facilitatorNotes: The Prince’s mother is named Luch, which means “the Mouse,” but real mice eat all the grain. Children can explain the joke in their own words.
evidence: The mouse shall have your grain.

days.title: A new home and a secret — excerpt
days.challenge: Notice how joy changes a character’s decision about privacy.
days.focus: Listen for the tension between hiding something and wanting to share it.
days.context: Johnny has secretly built a new home under an apple tree. His happiness soon meets a curious friend.
days.contentNote: This is a harmless surprise about an animal’s new home. Distinguish privacy from secrets about danger, which children should tell a trusted adult.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter VII; begins “Johnny Chuck pushed up the last bit of gravel …” and ends “… down the Lone Little Path onto the Green Meadows.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the planned back door harder to find than the front?
facilitatorNotes: He chooses a tall grass clump to hide it. The physical detail shows how much he values secrecy.
evidence: hidden behind a tall clump of meadow grass

questions.prompt: What makes Johnny want to share the secret after hiding his work so carefully?
facilitatorNotes: He is delighted and wants another person to enjoy it with him.
evidence: he must share it with some one

questions.prompt: What promise does Jimmy make before hearing the location?
facilitatorNotes: He says he will tell no one, reinforced by crossing his heart and repeated reminders.
evidence: he wouldn't tell a soul.

days.title: A secret travels — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow a chain of speakers while distinguishing accident from intention.
days.focus: Observe how one small disclosure multiplies.
days.context: Johnny has told only Jimmy about his hidden home. Jimmy has promised not to share the location.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter VII; begins “Jimmy Skunk was thinking so much about Johnny Chuck's …” and ends “… the house of old Mr. Toad and told him.”.

questions.prompt: How does Jimmy reveal the secret without deciding to announce it?
facilitatorNotes: He is preoccupied and answers Peter’s question before remembering the promise.
evidence: It just slipped out.

questions.prompt: What repeats when Peter next meets Reddy?
facilitatorNotes: Peter gives the destination, then covers his mouth and remembers it was secret, repeating Jimmy’s mistake.
evidence: clapped both hands over his mouth

questions.prompt: How is Reddy’s disclosure different from the first two?
facilitatorNotes: He refuses to promise silence and deliberately seeks someone to tell.
evidence: grinned a wicked grin and hurried off to find Bobby Coon

days.title: Everyone knows the hidden home — excerpt
