days.challenge: Connect an apparently puzzling saying with the events that explain it.
days.focus: Notice recovery from disappointment without pretending the loss did not matter.
days.context: The secret has passed from neighbor to neighbor. Johnny returns to his supposedly hidden house the next morning.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter VII; begins “The next morning, very early, before Old Mother West …” and ends “… round, red Mr. Sun has found it out yet.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Peter’s innocent appearance funny to a listener who heard the previous scene?
facilitatorNotes: We know he already learned and spread the location, although he acts as if he has just found it.
evidence: as if he had really just discovered the new home for the first time.

questions.prompt: What does Grandfather Frog mean by a whisper becoming a shout to the world?
facilitatorNotes: One listener tells another, so a private fact spreads widely without the first speaker addressing everyone.
evidence: Whisper a secret to a friend and you shout it in the ear of the whole world.

questions.prompt: How does the final question and answer protect Johnny’s next plan?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator refuses to reveal the new location, leaving the new secret intact.
evidence: Oh, that's Johnny Chuck's secret.

days.title: Saint Fronto’s Camels — Part 1: Hungry in the Desert
days.challenge: Understand two sides of a disagreement before the problem is solved.
days.focus: The hungry monks’ anger and Fronto’s trust set up the surprise that arrives at dawn.
days.context: Abbie Farwell Brown retold this saint legend for children in 1900. An oasis is a green, watered place in a desert. Nitria was a large monastery in Egypt.
days.contentNote: The monks have had only a few olives for many days and fear they will starve.

excerpt.locator: Saint Fronto’s Camels, from the opening; begins “THIS is a story of Egypt. In the midst …” and ends “… wept as he heard how faint their voices were.”.

questions.prompt: Why are the seventy monks angry with Fronto?
facilitatorNotes: He led them into the desert, promising they would be cared for, and now they are starving. They blame him for their suffering.
evidence: And they blamed one man for all their suffering.

questions.prompt: What does Fronto ask the monks to do, and what does he say he will do if no help comes?
facilitatorNotes: Wait until tomorrow; if help does not come they may go, but he will stay. Ask why he is so sure.
evidence: Wait till to-morrow. If help come not then, I give ye leave to go, without me.

questions.prompt: How does Fronto feel during the night, and what does he do?
facilitatorNotes: He feels sad and alone because his brothers have lost faith, and he prays all night. Children may think about how hard it is to wait.
evidence: All night he knelt on his goatskin mat praying

days.title: Saint Fronto’s Camels — Part 2: Bells at Dawn
days.challenge: Use sensory details to recognise a distant arrival gradually.
days.focus: Relief does not prevent the hungry people from caring for their helpers.
days.context: Fronto and the starving monks have agreed to wait one more night in their desert camp. At dawn an unexpected sound announces help.

excerpt.locator: Saint Fronto’s Camels — Part 1: Bells at Dawn; begins “At last the pink fingers of morning began to …” and ends “… and it explained how the camels had been sent.”.

questions.prompt: How does the arriving caravan change in Fronto’s sight as it comes nearer?
facilitatorNotes: It first looks like a dark thread or caterpillar, then becomes a line of rocking camels. Distance changes what can be recognised.
evidence: a thread of black, crawling like a caterpillar

questions.prompt: Why does Fronto look for a driver after the camels arrive?
facilitatorNotes: The animals appear to have travelled without a guide, which is the miracle claimed by this legend.
evidence: They had come all alone across the desert

questions.prompt: What do the monks do before opening their own breakfast?
facilitatorNotes: They unload the animals, wash feet, provide water and food, and make a shaded resting place. Their order of actions shows gratitude.
evidence: first of all the good monks tended the tired beasts

days.title: Saint Fronto’s Camels — Part 3: The Gift and the Meal
days.challenge: Follow a short backward look in time, then return to the present scene.
days.focus: A generous decision becomes a shared meal and another generous decision.
days.context: The camels have reached the hungry monks, who care for them first. A letter now explains the human giver behind the arrival.
days.contentNote: Hunger and religious trust are central to this legend. The unguided caravan is a miraculous story detail, not a safe travel plan.

excerpt.locator: Saint Fronto’s Camels — Part 2: The Gift and the Meal; begins “Four nights before this, Glaucus, the rich merchant, had …” and ends “… great waves between them and the world of cities.”.

questions.prompt: What contrast makes Glaucus decide to act after his dinner?
facilitatorNotes: He has enjoyed a feast and imagines the monks starving. His comfort makes him notice their possible need.
evidence: Perhaps they were starving now, while he was feasting.

questions.prompt: What does including hay for the camels tell us about the preparation?
facilitatorNotes: He plans for the animals’ needs as well as the human recipients; five loads are for the carriers themselves.
evidence: five of them with bales of hay for the camels themselves

questions.prompt: Why do the monks send half the provisions back?
facilitatorNotes: They believe the remaining food is more than enough for their simple meals. Discuss sharing surplus rather than assuming keeping everything is necessary.
evidence: half the provisions they returned

days.title: Saint Fronto’s Camels — Part 4: Humpo Comes Home
days.challenge: Recognise a repeated sound motif and a shift to another family’s viewpoint.
days.focus: A grand act of charity also involves one child’s affection for one animal.
days.context: Glaucus has sent food to the monks using seventy camels. Now his family waits for the animals’ return.

excerpt.locator: Saint Fronto’s Camels — Part 3: Humpo Comes Home; begins “Now it was eight days since Glaucus had sent …” and ends “… as eagerly as Santa Claus is at Christmas time.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Æmilia’s worry more personal than simply losing expensive animals?
facilitatorNotes: Humpo, the lead camel, is her favourite. She misses an individual companion.
evidence: The leader-camel was the favorite of Glaucus's daughter, Æmilia.

questions.prompt: What sound links the monks’ relief earlier with Æmilia’s relief now?
facilitatorNotes: The far-off bell tinkle announces the same caravan in both places; the repeated cue connects giver and receivers.
evidence: I think I hear the tinkle of a camel bell among the mountains!

questions.prompt: How does this one journey change what happens in later years?
facilitatorNotes: Glaucus sends the camels again each year, and the monks come to expect beloved visitors, not merely supplies.
evidence: every year after that he sent the seventy camels forth

days.title: The astonishing old suit — excerpt
days.challenge: Remember an unexpected answer that a character rejects.
days.focus: Read curiosity as both a motive and a source of comic disbelief.
days.context: Sleepy Peter walks home after a night outdoors and notices Mr. Toad looking different.
days.contentNote: Sammy and Peter exchange teasing insults. The animal’s “suit” is a story image for skin, not clothing to swallow.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter IX; begins “Peter Rabbit was tired and very sleepy as he …” and ends “… got to find out about Mr. Toad's old suit.”.

questions.prompt: What contrast between Peter and the Breezes marks the time of day?
facilitatorNotes: The Breezes are starting their day while Peter wants bed after being up all night.
evidence: Peter Rabbit was thinking of bed.

questions.prompt: What small observation turns a greeting into an investigation?
facilitatorNotes: Peter notices a new suit and asks what happened to the old one.
evidence: you have on a new suit

questions.prompt: Why does the answer fail to satisfy Peter even though Mr. Toad gives it directly?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot believe someone could swallow a suit, so his disbelief creates the mystery.
evidence: Of course he hadn't swallowed it!

days.title: A hungry storyteller — excerpt
days.challenge: Infer what one visitor notices and another misses.
days.focus: Contrast repeated questioning with attending to someone’s needs.
days.context: Peter asks Grandfather Frog to explain Mr. Toad’s old suit. The Breezes overhear and try another approach.
days.contentNote: Flies are eaten as part of this animal fantasy. Providing food before a story is a particular custom here, not a requirement for getting help.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter IX; begins “"I'll just run over to the Smiling Pool and …” and ends “… know what Mr. Toad did with his old suit.”.

questions.prompt: What does Peter fail to notice before asking his question?
facilitatorNotes: Grandfather Frog is hungry and has not caught flies yet; Peter is absorbed in his own curiosity.
evidence: Peter Rabbit was too full of curiosity in Mr. Toad's affairs to notice this.

questions.prompt: What do the Breezes do before asking the same question?
facilitatorNotes: They gather flies and blow them to the frog, attending to what Peter ignored.
evidence: each blowing ahead of him a fat, foolish, green fly

questions.prompt: How does the familiar story opening change their expectation?
facilitatorNotes: Once upon a time signals that a fuller explanation is coming, and they settle down to listen.
evidence: they knew that soon they would know

days.title: Fine work and fine clothes — excerpt
days.challenge: Compare a preparation everyone shares with one character’s different priority.
days.focus: Explore the story’s distinction between appearance and useful work.
days.context: Grandfather Frog tells an imaginary old story explaining the toad’s unusual way of changing his “suit.”
days.contentNote: The toad’s clothing is a fantasy image for shed skin. The magical explanation is not a scientific account, and people must not swallow clothing.

excerpt.locator: Mother West Wind’s Children, Chapter IX; begins “"Once upon a time," began Grandfather Frog again, "when …” and ends “… what old Mr. Toad did with his old suit.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Mr. Toad keep working in his old suit while everyone displays new clothes?
facilitatorNotes: He has a garden to tend and does not want work to spoil the new suit.
evidence: Mr. Toad had too much to do.

questions.prompt: What makes the supposedly perfect greeting comically imperfect?
facilitatorNotes: A trouser leg still sticks out of his mouth after he swallows the old suit.
evidence: a leg of his trousers hung out of a corner of his big mouth.

questions.prompt: What does Mother Nature reward despite that untidy detail?
facilitatorNotes: His hard work and well-kept garden, not flawless dress; the appointment identifies her priority.
evidence: I herewith appoint you my chief gardener

days.title: Saint Rigobert’s Dinner — Part 1: An Unexpected Gift
days.challenge: Read a child’s unspoken wishes through actions and expression.
days.focus: An offered meal becomes a difficult-to-carry living gift.
days.context: Abbie Farwell Brown retold this saint legend for children in 1900. Rigobert is a poor old bishop who has been sent away from court to a country village. Pierre is the boy who helps him.
days.contentNote: A live goose is intended as food, but it is not killed; later parts show its safe future. Hunger is real need, not a fault.

excerpt.locator: Saint Rigobert’s Dinner — Part 1: An Unexpected Gift; begins “SAINT RIGOBERT was hungry. He had eaten nothing that …” and ends “… grasping his staff, his eyes bent upon the ground.”.

questions.prompt: What shows that Pierre wants to stay even before he says anything?
facilitatorNotes: He trails behind, looks back toward the food, and later has tears of disappointment. These gestures convey hunger.
evidence: many a backward look

questions.prompt: Why does Rigobert refuse the meal although it is tempting?
facilitatorNotes: He says their service leaves too little time; the narrator also identifies his pride and wish not to expose the parish’s poverty. A child may notice both reasons with support.
evidence: he was too proud to accept charity

questions.prompt: Does the governor first think the goose is a valuable gift for himself?
facilitatorNotes: No; he complains that he already has too many birds, then offers it to Rigobert. His gift also solves his own inconvenience.
evidence: We have more fowls now than we know what to do with.

days.title: Saint Rigobert’s Dinner — Part 2: Let the Goose Go
days.challenge: Consider two feelings about a single event without dismissing either.
days.focus: Rigobert feels sympathy for both the hungry boy and the escaping bird.
days.context: Pierre is carrying the live goose promised for their dinner. On the road, the bird escapes from his arms.
days.contentNote: The boy is hungry and cries over losing a hoped-for meal. The bird escapes safely, and the following part resolves the dinner problem.

excerpt.locator: Saint Rigobert’s Dinner — Part 2: Let the Goose Go; begins “Pierre's heart was full of joy. He chuckled and …” and ends “… loved not to have creatures killed, even for food.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the same escape feel so different to Pierre and to the goose?
facilitatorNotes: Pierre loses the dinner he imagined; the goose gains freedom and avoids being roasted. The story lets both needs be seen.
evidence: perhaps the poor goose did not want to be roasted, Pierre

questions.prompt: How does Rigobert respond when Pierre blames himself?
facilitatorNotes: He comforts him and does not scold; he proposes trying to find something else.
evidence: I find no fault with him; but I am sorry for thy dinner, lad.

questions.prompt: What does Rigobert’s singing suggest as the two continue walking?
facilitatorNotes: It may steady their spirits and shows that he is not angry about the loss; the narrator suggests he is also glad for the bird. Accept tentative interpretations.
evidence: began to hum his hymns softly under his breath

days.title: Saint Rigobert’s Dinner — Part 3: A Friend and a Feast
days.challenge: Keep two linked resolutions in mind: the animal’s safety and the people’s hunger.
days.focus: A gift intended for eating becomes a friend, and neighbours respond with help.
days.context: The goose has escaped and Rigobert has comforted Pierre. As they walk on, the bird returns.
days.contentNote: Mentions the original plan to cook the goose; the animal is protected and nobody goes without the final meal.

excerpt.locator: Saint Rigobert’s Dinner — Part 3: A Friend and a Feast; begins “They had gone quite a little distance, and Rigobert …” and ends “… the house together to eat their good, good dinner.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Rigobert stop Pierre from grabbing the returning goose?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to see whether it will follow freely. That choice begins a friendship based on trust rather than confinement.
evidence: Do not touch him, Pierre

questions.prompt: What promise changes the goose’s place in the household?
facilitatorNotes: Rigobert promises it will not be plucked or cooked and may follow without a pen. It becomes a companion.
evidence: Thou art my friend from to-day.

questions.prompt: How is Pierre’s dinner problem finally solved?
facilitatorNotes: Neighbours hear what happened and bring food, also promising continuing help. The story does not require the boy simply to stay hungry.
evidence: they have sent us a basket of good things instead

days.title: Saint Francis of Assisi — Part 1: The Smile
days.challenge: Gather many examples that support one big idea about a person.
days.focus: The narrator describes Francis through his smile and his poverty before telling stories about him.
days.context: Abbie Farwell Brown retold these legends of Saint Francis for children in 1900. Francis lived in Assisi, in Italy, about eight hundred years ago. A crust is a dry piece of bread.

excerpt.locator: Saint Francis of Assisi, from the opening; begins “BAREFOOTED in the snow, bareheaded in the rain, Saint …” and ends “… many who love him like a lost elder brother.”.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator say Francis’s smile could do?
facilitatorNotes: It opened people’s hearts, comforted the sick and drew animals to him; the narrator calls it like a magic charm.
evidence: It was like a magic charm.

questions.prompt: What did Francis give away to save two lambs?
facilitatorNotes: His cloak, the only thing he had, to buy their lives; then he carried them home.
evidence: taking off his cloak, which was all he had to part with, he gave it to buy their lives

questions.prompt: Francis calls the Sun and the Wind his brothers and the Moon and Water his sisters. What does that show about how he saw the world?
facilitatorNotes: He felt related to everything, like one family. Children may give their own example of calling something brother or sister.
evidence: he called the Sun and Wind his brothers and the Moon and Water his sisters

days.title: Saint Francis of Assisi — Part 2: Taking Turns with the Birds
days.challenge: Notice polite dialogue and metaphors that give a setting new meaning.
days.focus: The birds and people make space for one another’s voices.
days.context: Francis teaches peace to people and, in these legends, to birds. The narrator treats the outdoor world as his church.

excerpt.locator: Saint Francis of Assisi — Taking Turns with the Birds; begins “Saint Francis preached to all lessons of charity and …” and ends “… and they went singing as he had bidden them.”.

questions.prompt: What becomes a roof, choir and congregation in Francis’s outdoor church?
facilitatorNotes: Sky is the roof, birds form a choir, and animals can be the listeners. The comparisons make the landscape feel like a gathering place.
evidence: the blue sky was the only roof between him and heaven

questions.prompt: Does Francis ask the birds to stop singing forever? How do you know?
facilitatorNotes: No; he asks them to wait for the brothers’ psalm, then they resume. The issue is taking turns.
evidence: when it was again their turn the birds went on with their song

questions.prompt: What gifts does his short bird-sermon ask the birds to notice?
facilitatorNotes: Feathers, wings, air and care are named; let the child recall two and connect them to gratitude in this religious setting.
evidence: clotheth you with feathers and giveth you wings to fly with

days.title: Saint Francis of Assisi — Part 3: Brother Wolf
days.challenge: Follow both sides of an agreement and how each side keeps it.
days.focus: A frightening wolf becomes a neighbour when Francis arranges a promise between the wolf and the town.
days.context: Francis has preached peace to people and to birds. Gubbio is a town in Italy. A surety is someone who promises that an agreement will be kept.
days.contentNote: The legend says the wolf had killed sheep, cows and people before Francis made peace with him; this is told in one sentence.

excerpt.locator: Saint Francis of Assisi, the Wolf of Gubbio; begins “Saint Francis preached the lessons of peace; he would …” and ends “… power the humble beast had been a daily reminder.”.

questions.prompt: Why were the people of Gubbio afraid to leave their town?
facilitatorNotes: A huge wolf stole animals and even carried off people. That is why the townsfolk begged Francis not to go out.
evidence: he came and carried off men also for his dinner

questions.prompt: What promise do the wolf and the people make to each other?
facilitatorNotes: The wolf will never harm anyone, and the people will give him his food every day; Francis stands as surety for him.
evidence: if ye promise to give him day by day what is needful for his dinner

questions.prompt: How did the people feel when Brother Wolf died, and why?
facilitatorNotes: They were sorrowful, because they missed his footsteps and grieved for Francis’s loss of a friend. Their enemy had become a friend.
evidence: the citizens were very sorrowful

days.title: Saint Francis of Assisi — Part 4: The Little Hare and the Mountain
days.challenge: Infer trust from repeated animal actions.
days.focus: Protection means eventually helping the creature return to its own home.
days.context: Francis cares for creatures in trouble. Later, old and tired, he receives a quiet mountain from a nobleman named Orlando.
days.contentNote: A live hare is brought for breakfast but is set free unharmed. Francis is old and unwell at the end of this part.

excerpt.locator: Saint Francis of Assisi — The Little Hare; begins “Francis could not bear to see a little brother …” and ends “… childlike, simple, happy little brother, Saint Francis of Assisi.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the hare keep coming back after being set free?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator suggests it feels safe with its rescuer. Point to its return and hiding rather than claiming to know every real hare’s feelings.
evidence: Again and again it returned nestling to its new-found friend

questions.prompt: How does Francis solve the problem without keeping the hare permanently?
facilitatorNotes: He sends a companion to return it to the woods among other hares. Caring includes restoring its freedom.
evidence: safe once more among its little bob-tailed brothers and sisters

questions.prompt: Why is a bare mountain a precious gift to Francis?
facilitatorNotes: He is worn from travelling and loves wild creatures; the quiet place gives rest and closeness to them, even without a house.
evidence: a bare and lonely mountain top where wild beasts lived and wild birds had a home

questions.prompt: How does the birds’ arrival affect the peasant differently from Francis’s companions?
facilitatorNotes: The companions have seen similar scenes, but the peasant is astonished and cannot believe his eyes.
evidence: stood like one turned to stone

days.title: An invitation and an anxious song — excerpt
days.challenge: Hear imagined objections woven into a song.
days.focus: Contrast an invitation’s purpose with worries about being overlooked.
days.context: The flood has ended. Christopher Robin plans a party to thank Pooh for helping Piglet.

excerpt.locator: Winnie-the-Pooh, Chapter X; begins “One day when the sun had come back over …” and ends “… shall come. Only don't blame me if it rains."”.

questions.prompt: What does the peaceful forest opening tell us about the flood?
facilitatorNotes: Streams have returned to their usual shape, and the forest has become warm and quiet.
evidence: their own pretty shape again

questions.prompt: What is Pooh afraid the other animals will forget?
facilitatorNotes: That he rescued Piglet and the party celebrates that act; the song gives forgetting an answering voice.
evidence: nobody quite knew what the party was for

questions.prompt: Why does Owl have to repeat that Eeyore is invited?
facilitatorNotes: Eeyore assumes he is excluded and imagines the message was meant for Piglet; the repetition makes inclusion explicit.
evidence: All of them! Tell all of them.

days.title: A present and a walk home — excerpt
days.challenge: Follow a misunderstanding until a concrete announcement resolves it.
days.focus: Notice how a gift and a quiet conversation express belonging.
days.context: The friends are at Pooh’s thank-you party. A speech temporarily confuses whose party it is; the closing scene returns to Christopher Robin and the narrator.
days.contentNote: The gift includes a pencil-sharpening knife; the scene describes a historical present, not a child activity.

excerpt.locator: Winnie-the-Pooh, Chapter X; begins “But it didn't rain. Christopher Robin had made a …” and ends “… heard Winnie-the-Pooh—bump, bump, bump—going up the stairs behind him.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Pooh briefly think the party may belong to Eeyore?
facilitatorNotes: Eeyore’s speech calls it his own party while Christopher Robin is searching for the present.
evidence: to see you at my party

questions.prompt: What do the pencil labels mean to the friends rather than to a pencil maker?
facilitatorNotes: B, HB, and BB become Bear, Helping Bear, and Brave Bear, celebrating Pooh through playful interpretations.
evidence: "HB" for Helping Bear

questions.prompt: Why can Pooh call breakfast and an exciting new day “the same thing”?
facilitatorNotes: For him breakfast is an eagerly awaited adventure; accept an affectionate reading of his dependable pleasures.
evidence: "It's the same thing," he said.

days.title: Saint Launomar’s Cow — Part 1: The Night Robbers
days.challenge: Track how a captured animal turns the tables on her captors.
days.focus: The robbers make a mistake by trusting the cow, and Mignon decides how to use her freedom.
days.context: Abbie Farwell Brown retold this saint legend for children in 1900. Launomar lives in a monastery near Chartres in France. Mignon is his clever cow. A halter is a rope for leading an animal.
days.contentNote: Five robbers with knives steal the cow and tie her mouth shut; she leads them through mud and brambles all night until they are scratched and worn out.

excerpt.locator: Saint Launomar’s Cow, from the opening; begins “SAINT LAUNOMAR had once been a shepherd boy in …” and ends “… bleeding from the briars, and cross as ten sticks.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the robbers tie up Mignon’s mouth?
facilitatorNotes: So she cannot moo and wake the monastery. Mignon had planned to do exactly that.
evidence: so that she could not low and tell the whole monastery what danger she was in

questions.prompt: Why do the robbers decide to let the cow lead the way?
facilitatorNotes: They are lost and quarrelling about directions, and one says animals can lead you aright in the dark.
evidence: Let us follow the cow

questions.prompt: What does Mignon decide to do with the robbers, and is it fair?
facilitatorNotes: She leads them round and round through mud, brambles and ponds all night to punish them. Children may think it is fair, too harsh, or clever; ask for reasons.
evidence: I must punish them all I can now that it is my turn.

days.title: Saint Launomar’s Cow — Part 2: The Return and the Breakfast
days.challenge: Use the difference between characters’ beliefs and the later reveal.
days.focus: A cow’s clever route and a man’s unexpected courtesy bring the theft to an end.
days.context: Mignon has led the five robbers round and round through the forest all night. At sunrise they think they are nearing their own home.
days.contentNote: The robbers are scratched and cross from the night; the theft is discussed and the men apologise.

excerpt.locator: Saint Launomar’s Cow — The Return and the Breakfast; begins “But when at last, an hour after sunrise, Mignon …” and ends “And they both chuckled inside.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the robbers’ confident talk about being far away funny after the reveal?
facilitatorNotes: They believe they have travelled twenty-five miles toward safety, but the cow has kept them near the monastery. Distance walked is not the same as getting far from the start.
evidence: they were no farther on their journey than they had been at the start

questions.prompt: Does Launomar’s kind greeting mean he has no idea what happened?
facilitatorNotes: No; footprints have already told him about the theft. His politeness is a chosen response, not simple ignorance.
evidence: her footprints with those of the five robbers in the moist earth had told the story

questions.prompt: How does breakfast make the men face what they almost took away?
facilitatorNotes: They eat food made with Mignon’s milk, while Launomar explains her value as friend and provider. The meal joins generosity with a reminder of responsibility.
evidence: That is Mignon's milk which you drink, Sirs.

days.title: The Island
days.challenge: Picture a place described through color, distance, and a speaker’s imagined position.
days.focus: A private daydream makes a large seascape feel personally owned.
days.context: This whole poem imagines sailing to an island, climbing a cliff, and resting above the sea. Its Eastern seas are the speaker’s broad imagined setting; no particular real island is identified. An adult reads the poem; the child may join the repeated ship and climbing phrases.

excerpt.locator: The Island; begins 'THE ISLAND'; ends 'And I’d say to myself as I looked so lazily down at the sea:\n“There’s nobody else in the world, and the world was made for me.”'. Source block range 130–132 in the documented transcription extraction.

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker imagine resting their chin?
facilitatorNotes: In their hands, while gazing down toward sand and waves. Invite the child to show the pose.
evidence: My chin in my hands

questions.prompt: Which words make the far distance look different from the near sand?
facilitatorNotes: The near sand dazzles; the distance is grey-blue haze. Compare the two without needing a drawing.
evidence: the grey-blue distant haze

questions.prompt: Must the final claim about nobody else be literally true?
facilitatorNotes: No; it can express the feeling of perfect solitude in a daydream. The conditional I’d say helps us hear an imagined moment.
evidence: the world was made for me

days.title: Granny’s Wonderful Chair — Part 1: The Chair’s Secret
days.challenge: Remember two different instructions for one magical object.
days.focus: Storytelling gives company, and practical preparation begins an adventure.
days.context: Frances Browne’s book of fairy tales. Snowflower and her grandmother live beside a forest. A spinning wheel makes yarn; a chair with wheels is about to prove much more unusual.
days.contentNote: A child is left alone and runs low on food; this is a fantasy situation, not an example of suitable childcare. The bird and cat departures are imagined animal behaviour.

excerpt.locator: Granny’s Wonderful Chair — Part 1: The Chair’s Secret; begins “In an old time, long ago, when the fairies …” and ends “… of my grandmother, take me the way she went."”.

questions.prompt: What does Snowflower receive each evening that is precious although it costs no money?
facilitatorNotes: Her grandmother tells a new story; later the chair continues that companionship. Invite the child to notice comfort alongside the family’s real need for food.
evidence: Dame Frostyface set aside her wheel, and told her a new story.

questions.prompt: How does Snowflower show thanks to a voice whose owner she cannot find?
facilitatorNotes: She cares for the chair by polishing the back and dusting the cushion. Her actions address the place from which the voice comes.
evidence: polishing up the oaken back, and dusting the velvet cushion

questions.prompt: Why does she decide it is time to use the chair for travel?
facilitatorNotes: The food is nearly gone and her grandmother has not returned; she hopes to find advice. She oils the wheels as instructed before leaving.
evidence: perhaps she would advise me what to do

days.title: Granny’s Wonderful Chair — Part 2: A Splendid, Unwelcoming City
days.challenge: Compare impressive descriptions with the way people actually behave.
days.focus: Rich surroundings do not guarantee a generous welcome.
days.context: Snowflower has oiled the magical chair and asked it to follow her grandmother. Its journey reaches workers preparing a royal feast.
days.contentNote: The king’s brother is missing, and the child encounters class prejudice. Includes non-graphic mention of animals being prepared for a feast.

excerpt.locator: Granny’s Wonderful Chair — Part 2: A Splendid, Unwelcoming City; begins “Presently the chair gave a creak, and began to …” and ends “… and eat up the scraps the cook threw away.”.

questions.prompt: What changes Snowflower’s destination from her grandmother’s path to the palace?
facilitatorNotes: She hears about a feast open to everybody and hopes to share it after eating only barley cakes.
evidence: perhaps share in, such a noble feast

questions.prompt: Which detail about the city surprises Snowflower despite all its wealth?
facilitatorNotes: Many people look dissatisfied and greedy. The contrast unsettles the idea that splendid possessions always bring contentment.
evidence: so many discontented, covetous faces

questions.prompt: How does the treatment of Snowflower fail to match the promise that everybody will be feasted?
facilitatorNotes: She is placed in the worst kitchen with scraps rather than welcomed as a guest. Invite a fairer alternative grounded in what happens.
evidence: eat up the scraps the cook threw away

days.title: Granny’s Wonderful Chair — Part 3: A Story for the King
days.challenge: Follow a chain of messengers and recognise a repeated request.
days.focus: The disregarded guest has something the splendid feast cannot supply.
days.context: Snowflower has been allowed to stay in the palace kitchen. The grand feast is beginning, but the king and his guests are unhappy.
days.contentNote: People treat Snowflower unfairly because she is poor; the passage invites noticing that injustice.

excerpt.locator: Granny’s Wonderful Chair — Part 3: A Story for the King; begins “That very day the feast began; it was fine …” and ends “… cushion, said:—"Listen to the story of the Christmas Cuckoo!"”.

questions.prompt: Why is there so little merriment at a feast full of food and music?
facilitatorNotes: Guests compare their rooms and finery, servants want presents, and people outside demand the return of property. Name one concrete complaint.
evidence: others were vexed to see many finer than themselves

questions.prompt: What is funny or surprising about how the king’s short command reaches Snowflower?
facilitatorNotes: It passes through many people, from page and messenger to cooks and dust-boy. Retelling the chain shows the palace’s elaborate hierarchy.
evidence: the chief-scullion told the dust-boy, and he told Snowflower

questions.prompt: Does Snowflower need a new way to ask for a story in the grand hall?
facilitatorNotes: No; she rests her head and uses the same familiar words as at home. The repeated action connects cottage and palace.
evidence: as she used to do in the old cottage

days.title: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 1: A Guest in the Log
days.challenge: Trace a practical problem into a surprising fantasy encounter.
days.focus: A warm fire becomes an opportunity to offer shelter.
days.context: The wonderful chair begins a tale of two poor brothers who mend shoes. A yule log is a large log burned for a Christmas fire.
days.contentNote: Contains a hearth fire and adults drinking beer. The cuckoo emerges unharmed. Its long sleep in a log and speech are make-believe.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 1: A Guest in the Log; begins “"Once upon a time there stood in the midst …” and ends “… scooped for him in the thatch of the hut.”.

questions.prompt: Why are the brothers especially short of money this winter?
facilitatorNotes: A skilled new cobbler takes their customers and bad weather harms their crops. Their hardship has several causes rather than a single mistake.
evidence: The season had been wet and cold, their barley did not ripen well

questions.prompt: How do Scrub and Spare respond differently when the log calls “Cuckoo”?
facilitatorNotes: Scrub assumes something bad; Spare leaves open another explanation, then welcomes the bird. Both are surprised.
evidence: May be not

questions.prompt: What does Spare give the bird besides permission to stay?
facilitatorNotes: He offers barley bread and makes a snug sleeping hole in the thatch. These details turn welcome into care.
evidence: a snug hole which Spare scooped for him in the thatch

days.title: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 2: Two Different Wishes
days.challenge: Compare two gifts whose value is measured in different ways.
days.focus: A choice reveals what each brother hopes will improve his life.
days.context: The bird has spent the winter in the brothers’ roof. As spring returns it offers a gift for their hospitality.
days.contentNote: Poverty and exclusion continue while the brothers wait. The leaves’ promised effects are magical, not a rule that people should ignore difficult feelings.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 2: Two Different Wishes; begins “"Scrub said he was afraid it wouldn't be lucky; …” and ends “… beak knocking at their door, and a voice crying—”.

questions.prompt: Which changes tell us that winter has given way to spring?
facilitatorNotes: Snow melts, cold lessens and days lengthen before the bird announces spring. Let the child choose two concrete signs.
evidence: the days lengthened

questions.prompt: Why can the cuckoo offer leaves but not the jewels Scrub first requests?
facilitatorNotes: It says its knowledge concerns things growing on earth, while diamonds and pearls are elsewhere. This limit makes the two tree choices important.
evidence: My knowledge is only of that which grows on the earth.

questions.prompt: What does Spare want that the golden leaf does not promise?
facilitatorNotes: The merry leaf promises a cheerful heart through difficulties, even in a hut. Scrub chooses material wealth instead; let the child explain the difference without requiring one simple moral.
evidence: as merry in a hut as in a palace

days.title: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 3: The Gifts Arrive
days.challenge: Distinguish what characters assume from what the story has yet to show.
days.focus: Quick judgments about value begin to separate the brothers.
days.context: A year after the brothers chose gifts, the cuckoo knocks with a gold leaf for Scrub and a green one for Spare.
days.contentNote: Scrub insults his brother and excludes him from a wedding. The story presents these as actions to consider, not models of family kindness.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 3: The Gifts Arrive; begins “"'Cuckoo! cuckoo! Let me in with my presents.'” and ends “… his brother thought him a disgrace to the family.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Scrub welcome a thick slice of bread for the cuckoo this time?
facilitatorNotes: He has just received valuable gold and feels pleased; compare this with his earlier concern over sharing bread.
evidence: So much gold had never been in the cobbler's hands before

questions.prompt: Does the cuckoo agree that Spare’s choice is foolish? What words show its response?
facilitatorNotes: It calls Scrub’s conclusions hasty and discourteous, leaving room for the green leaf’s value to appear later.
evidence: your conclusions are more hasty than courteous

questions.prompt: What changes in the villagers’ treatment of Scrub when he shows the gold?
facilitatorNotes: They praise him, offer work and a partnership, and celebrate his marriage. Their approval follows visible wealth.
evidence: The new cobbler immediately took him into partnership

days.title: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 4: Visitors to the Hut
days.challenge: Follow a change that spreads from one person to others.
days.focus: The value of company becomes visible in how visitors treat people afterward.
days.context: Scrub spends a gold leaf each year, while Spare keeps his green leaves in the old hut. Different kinds of visitors begin to seek Spare’s company.
days.contentNote: The narrator uses dated disability language and describes a woman unfairly called a witch because she is old and considered ugly. Appearance and age provide no evidence of wrongdoing. Magical cheerfulness is not a cure for illness.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 4: Visitors to the Hut; begins “"Indeed, all who heard the story concluded that Spare …” and ends “… a command that he should repair to court immediately.”.

questions.prompt: Why are Scrub and Fairfeather still dissatisfied after buying fine things?
facilitatorNotes: The gold is used up piece by piece before the next leaf arrives. Their purchases do not end wanting.
evidence: neither she nor Scrub were content

questions.prompt: What specific change in one of Spare’s friends shows that his company affects more than appearances?
facilitatorNotes: The tinker treats his donkey more kindly, the boy avoids mischief, or the woman is gentler with cat and children. Any one example supports an answer.
evidence: the tinker grew kinder to the poor ass

questions.prompt: How does the great lord’s changed mood affect travellers and poor people?
facilitatorNotes: He welcomes them to his hall instead of remaining shut inside his grievances. The change becomes hospitality.
evidence: all travellers were entertained and all the poor were welcome

days.title: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 5: A Coat Worth Keeping
days.challenge: Connect an apparently shabby object with information other characters lack.
days.focus: Remembering an earlier life matters even after receiving grand gifts.
days.context: A royal messenger has invited Spare to court. He delays departure until the cuckoo’s yearly visit and carries its leaves sewn into his old coat.
days.contentNote: The bird fears being caught at court. “Doublet” means a fitted coat; its hidden magical leaves belong to the fantasy.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 5: A Coat Worth Keeping; begins “"'To-morrow is the first of April,' said Spare, 'and …” and ends “… leaves, because he had none to carry for Spare.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Spare wait until after sunrise on the first of April?
facilitatorNotes: That is when the cuckoo brings its leaf; he wants to see his friend before leaving.
evidence: the cuckoo came at sunrise with the merry leaf

questions.prompt: Why is the large farewell slice of bread a telling detail?
facilitatorNotes: Spare gives generously despite having only a brief visit, unlike Scrub’s earlier resentment about sharing. It shows continuing gratitude.
evidence: it was so thick and large

questions.prompt: The servants think the coat is mean. What reasons does Spare give for keeping it?
facilitatorNotes: It is comfortable and recalls his earlier life. Listeners also know that it holds the leaves, a reason the court does not hear.
evidence: recalling the days when it was my holiday garment

days.title: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 6: Golden Leaves and a Wood-Witch
days.challenge: Notice how flattery makes characters believe something untrue about themselves.
days.focus: Scrub and Fairfeather’s dream of grandeur makes them easy to trick.
days.context: Spare has gone to the king’s court with his merry green leaves sewn into his old coat. Scrub and Fairfeather, who chose golden leaves, hear about his success. Mead is a strong drink made from honey; a doublet is a fitted coat.
days.contentNote: A wood-witch gives Scrub and Fairfeather a sleeping drink and her two dwarf sons rob them.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Cuckoo; begins “"'Think of that!' said Fairfeather. 'Here we are spending …” and ends “… had carried like a bundle on his little back.”.

questions.prompt: Why do Scrub and Fairfeather set out for the king’s palace?
facilitatorNotes: They think their golden leaves will make the king give them titles, fine clothes and presents.
evidence: I'm sure he will make you a lord and me a lady of honour

questions.prompt: How does the old woman trick them?
facilitatorNotes: She flatters them as lord and lady and gives them her mead, which makes drinkers fall asleep and dream with open eyes while her sons rob them.
evidence: had the power of making all who drank it fall asleep and dream with their eyes open

questions.prompt: What does Spy bring home, and why is it important to the story?
facilitatorNotes: Spare’s old leathern doublet with the merry leaves in it. The listener knows it is magic, but the witch thinks it is worthless.
evidence: And he tossed down Spare's doublet, with the merry leaves in it

days.title: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 7: The Lost Doublet
days.challenge: Compare what happens to two people when one coat changes owners.
days.focus: The doublet’s magic moves with it: Scrub becomes merry while Spare loses his place at court.
days.context: The witch’s son Spy has found Spare’s leathern doublet. Now the story explains how it came to be thrown away. A page is a young servant; to confiscate is to take away someone’s goods.
days.contentNote: In a temper Scrub vows to take the old woman’s life but does nothing; a crowd is ready to stone Spare, who escapes from a window.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Cuckoo; begins “"To explain how Spy came by it, I must …” and ends “… the end of this lane,' and he trudged away.”.

questions.prompt: Why did the page Tinseltoes throw Spare’s doublet out of the window?
facilitatorNotes: He thought the old leather coat was unfashionable and made people remember Spare had been a cobbler.
evidence: but for it he was persuaded people would never remember that Spare had been a cobbler

questions.prompt: What changes for Scrub as soon as he buttons on the doublet?
facilitatorNotes: He becomes merry, makes Fairfeather laugh, and they live happily in the forest without worrying about their losses.
evidence: Scarcely was it buttoned on when a change came over him

questions.prompt: What happens at court once the doublet is gone?
facilitatorNotes: Quarrels and jealousies return, and Spare is banished. Ask the child to connect the court’s change to the missing leaves.
evidence: That very day things came back to their old fashion.

days.title: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 8: The Forest Meeting
days.challenge: Use knowledge shared with the listener but not with every character.
days.focus: An unexpected welcome reveals how a person has changed.
days.context: Spare has escaped from court and is searching the forest for his doublet. Scrub and Fairfeather are living in a hut of boughs, and Scrub is wearing the doublet.
days.contentNote: Food is cooked over a fire in the forest.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Cuckoo — The Forest Meeting; begins “"Determined to find his doublet, and sure that neither …” and ends “… his life, though we live in this poor hut.'”.

questions.prompt: What helps Spare find shelter when he cannot see a path to a house?
facilitatorNotes: A red firelight shines through the thicket. The sensory detail turns an uncertain dark journey toward a meeting.
evidence: the red light of a fire, gleaming through a thicket

questions.prompt: Why does Fairfeather not greet Spare as a relative at first?
facilitatorNotes: His life at court has changed his appearance; she does not recognise him. The listener knows more than she does.
evidence: Fairfeather did not know him

questions.prompt: What has changed in Fairfeather’s manner since the wedding that excluded Spare?
facilitatorNotes: She politely invites the stranger to share supper and adds more eggs. This welcome contrasts with her earlier pride.
evidence: Sit down and have a share of our supper

days.title: The Christmas Cuckoo — Part 9: Home with Three Leaves
days.challenge: Compare a character’s stated fortune with what others expect fortune to mean.
days.focus: A reunion changes the family’s choice of gifts and their everyday work.
days.context: Spare has found his brother and Fairfeather living in a forest hut, with his missing coat. She still does not recognise their guest.

excerpt.locator: The Christmas Cuckoo — Home with Three Leaves; begins “"'It is a shabby doublet, that,' said Spare, taking …” and ends “… I last heard the news of the north country."”.

questions.prompt: Why does Fairfeather think exchanging the coat for Spare’s cloak is an excellent bargain?
facilitatorNotes: The cloak looks rich; she does not know the green leaves are sewn inside the old coat. Different knowledge creates different judgments.
evidence: seeing that it was his own, for the merry leaves were still sewed in its lining

questions.prompt: What does Spare mean when he says he has made his fortune?
facilitatorNotes: He means recovering his own coat, not collecting new money or rank. Ask the child to connect the answer to what the coat contains.
evidence: in getting back my own good leathern doublet

questions.prompt: How do the final three leaves show that Scrub and Fairfeather have changed their minds?
facilitatorNotes: They now choose merry leaves along with Spare instead of gold; the annual gift includes all three.
evidence: Scrub and Fairfeather would have no more golden ones

days.title: Granny’s Wonderful Chair — Scarlet Shoes for Snowflower
days.challenge: Move from an embedded story back to its listeners.
days.focus: Different responses reveal what people took from the same tale.
days.context: The chair has just finished the Christmas Cuckoo tale, ending with a happy family in a flowering hut. Snowflower and the royal listeners respond.
days.contentNote: Mentions ale being given to a child, a historical story detail rather than suitable present-day practice.

excerpt.locator: Granny’s Wonderful Chair — Scarlet Shoes for Snowflower; begins “"What a summer-house that hut would make for me, …” and ends “… under the cushion, "to the story of Lady Greensleeves."”.

questions.prompt: What does the princess notice about the hut, and how is that different from the family’s enjoyment of it?
facilitatorNotes: She wants it as her own summer-house; the family valued shared life there. The queen even proposes moving it bodily.
evidence: What a summer-house that hut would make for me, mamma!

questions.prompt: What makes the tale seem connected to people in the banquet hall?
facilitatorNotes: Three richly dressed listeners stand and identify it as their story. This moment joins the magical story and its surrounding setting.
evidence: That's our story.

questions.prompt: Do the new shoes immediately change the way the kitchen treats Snowflower?
facilitatorNotes: Only partly, if at all: she still sleeps on straw and receives scraps. The gift is splendid, but equal welcome has not arrived.
evidence: allowed to sleep on some straw at the kitchen fire

days.title: The Mirror

questions.prompt: How do we know the sea is noisy without hearing a recording?

questions.prompt: What does calling the sea galloping make you picture?

days.title: Merrymind — Part 1: One Silver Penny
days.challenge: Distinguish wanting many attractive things from choosing one particular thing.
days.focus: A small amount of money creates a meaningful choice.
days.context: The chair’s next tale follows the youngest of thirteen children to a fair held only once in seven years. A “fairing” is a purchase or present from a fair.
days.contentNote: Adults buy tobacco-related objects, a historical detail rather than an endorsement. The neighbours’ belief that a name is “above” the family’s station reflects class prejudice.

excerpt.locator: Merrymind — Part 1: One Silver Penny; begins “"Once upon a time there lived in the north …” and ends “… go home at sunset, because the way was long.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the father give each child a penny even though money is scarce?
facilitatorNotes: The fair is rare, and he wants them to have something to spend on this special occasion. Notice both generosity and the family’s limited resources.
evidence: as the fair happened only once in seven years

questions.prompt: Which details help you imagine the fair as more than a row of shops?
facilitatorNotes: Puppet shows, rope dancers, tents, crowds and conversations give sights, movement and social life. Ask the child to choose one to picture or act out.
evidence: the puppet-shows, the rope-dancers

questions.prompt: Why is Merrymind the only one with his penny left near evening?
facilitatorNotes: He wants a fiddle, but none he has priced costs as little as his penny. Waiting is connected with a particular wish.
evidence: he had set his heart upon a fiddle

days.title: Merrymind — Part 2: The Broken Fiddle
days.challenge: Notice important information disclosed only after a bargain is made.
days.focus: A cheap purchase carries an unexpected problem.
days.context: Merrymind has saved his penny for a fiddle, but the instruments he has seen cost too much. Near closing time he finds an overlooked stall.

excerpt.locator: Merrymind — Part 2: The Broken Fiddle; begins “"The sun was getting low and red upon the …” and ends “… and up the hill he ran like a greyhound.”.

questions.prompt: How is the little man’s stall different from the busy merchant’s nearby?
facilitatorNotes: It has only one old fiddle with broken strings, while the merchant’s fine new goods attract customers. The contrast helps explain why Merrymind can afford it.
evidence: nothing on his stall but one old dingy fiddle

questions.prompt: Why does Merrymind think the broken strings will not matter much?
facilitatorNotes: He is handy and expects to mend them while watching sheep. His plan depends on an assumption about ordinary repairs.
evidence: could mend the strings while watching his father's sheep

questions.prompt: What important fact does the seller tell him only after the purchase and packing?
facilitatorNotes: Only night-spinners’ threads will mend the fiddle. Invite the child to say why that information would have helped before paying.
evidence: except by threads from the night-spinners

days.title: Merrymind — Part 3: A Hope Worth Carrying
days.challenge: Compare criticism that labels a person with a response that leaves room to learn.
days.focus: One person’s encouragement helps a disappointed child keep trying.
days.context: The seller has revealed that only mysterious night-spinners’ threads can repair the fiddle. Merrymind returns home with his purchase.
days.contentNote: The family and neighbours ridicule a child and he leaves home. Their unkindness is open to criticism; real children deserve support and safe adult care.

excerpt.locator: Merrymind — Part 3: A Hope Worth Carrying; begins “"Merrymind thought that was queer news, but being given …” and ends “… summer morning with the broken-stringed fiddle under his arm.”.

questions.prompt: How does the mother’s response differ from the father’s prediction?
facilitatorNotes: The father predicts lasting poor judgment from one purchase; the mother says the next choice may be better and the fiddle may yet help. She leaves room for growth.
evidence: if he laid out one penny ill, he might lay out the next better

questions.prompt: What makes Merrymind begin asking about night-spinners instead of trying ordinary repairs forever?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated mending fails; the seller’s strange statement begins to fit the evidence.
evidence: no mending would stand, and no string would hold

questions.prompt: What object does Merrymind choose to carry when he sets out, and what does that choice show?
facilitatorNotes: He keeps the fiddle, showing hope and attachment despite ridicule. The departure is fantasy adventure, not a suggestion that children should leave home.
evidence: with the broken-stringed fiddle under his arm

days.title: Merrymind — Part 4: The Heavy Pannier
days.challenge: Track how an offered kindness becomes more difficult than expected.
days.focus: A remembered song creates a pause in a harsh encounter.
days.context: Merrymind travels with his broken fiddle, hoping to find the seller or the night-spinners. At two paths he meets a burdened stranger. A pannier is a large carrying basket.
days.contentNote: A stranger insults the boy and ties him to a basket until night, then releases him; no injury is described. Offering help does not oblige someone to accept mistreatment. This is a fantasy journey, not travel guidance.

excerpt.locator: Merrymind — Part 4: The Heavy Pannier; begins “"There were no highways then in the north country—people …” and ends “… with his fiddle close by, he fell fast asleep.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Merrymind choose the rough path rather than the green-looking wood?
facilitatorNotes: He offers to help the older man carry a burden because he thinks the man is tired. The choice comes from concern, though the stranger behaves badly.
evidence: you seem tired, and I am younger than you

questions.prompt: What does singing change during the difficult walk?
facilitatorNotes: The man stops scolding and later notices that nobody has sung while helping him before. Merrymind uses a rhyme learned from his mother.
evidence: no one ever sang while helping me before

questions.prompt: Why might Merrymind choose an empty cold cottage over the man’s kitchen fire?
facilitatorNotes: He has had enough of the man’s harsh company and chooses distance. The text supports preferring a less comfortable place that feels more peaceful.
evidence: he had got quite enough of the old man's society

days.title: Merrymind — Part 5: A Valley without Laughter
days.challenge: Notice a repeated pattern across people, animals and buildings.
days.focus: Abundant possessions cannot replace rest, conversation and enjoyment.
days.context: After the difficult journey, Merrymind sleeps in an empty cottage. He hears mysterious singing in his dreams and wakes to explore the valley.
days.contentNote: Children are shown working without play, and the narrator uses a dated disability label. The passage criticises the valley’s relentless labour; a person’s disability does not determine character.

excerpt.locator: Merrymind — Part 5: A Valley without Laughter; begins “"The floor was hard, and his clothes were thin, …” and ends “… if they have always worked so hard and heavily.'”.

questions.prompt: What is puzzling about Merrymind’s memory of the night when he wakes?
facilitatorNotes: He remembers singing and spinning, but the house is bare and solitary. The difference creates a mystery rather than proving it was only a dream.
evidence: singing voices and spinning-wheels

questions.prompt: Why does Merrymind think the people’s endless work is unreasonable?
facilitatorNotes: They already appear rich and have fine possessions, yet never enjoy them. Their activity seems disconnected from making life pleasant.
evidence: their owners took neither ease nor pleasure in them

questions.prompt: What has happened to the castle’s banquet hall, where you might expect a feast?
facilitatorNotes: It has become a place for churning and cheesemaking. The changed use extends the valley’s work into a space intended for gathering.
evidence: They were churning in the banquet hall.

days.title: Merrymind — Part 6: Questions at the Gate
days.challenge: Follow questions that become more urgent as new information appears.
days.focus: One person willing to talk can reveal a problem hidden by constant activity.
days.context: Nobody in the valley has time to answer Merrymind. Night brings another unexplained sound of singing, and the next day he searches farther.
days.contentNote: Merrymind learns that he is not free to leave. The soldier has one arm and smokes a pipe. At night a giant chases the boy away with stones.

excerpt.locator: Merrymind — Part 6: Questions at the Gate; begins “"By this time the night again came on: he …” and ends “… him bad names, half way back to the cottage.”.

questions.prompt: What words tell Merrymind that play is excluded from the valley’s routine?
facilitatorNotes: The old man describes only work by day and sleep by night, and rejects sport. Ask what this leaves out of life.
evidence: There is no sport in Dame Dreary's land!

questions.prompt: Why does the soldier look like a possible friend before Merrymind knows him?
facilitatorNotes: He is the first person not busy working, so he may have time to answer. The hope is based on the day’s repeated refusals.
evidence: He was the first idle man Merrymind had seen in the valley

questions.prompt: What is unfair about the soldier’s orders at the gate?
facilitatorNotes: People may enter but cannot leave, so Merrymind did not knowingly agree to stay. The answer is supported by the rule’s unequal directions.
evidence: to let everybody in and nobody out

questions.prompt: What does the soldier say will make the valley merry again?
facilitatorNotes: Dame Dreary must lay down her distaff and dance. Many fiddlers have tried and failed, which raises the question of what Merrymind can do.
evidence: They say it will be so till Dame Dreary lays down her distaff, and dances

days.title: Merrymind — The Night-Spinners’ Gift
days.challenge: Connect a long-remembered clue with a newly recognised opportunity.
days.focus: A useful gift is exchanged for care, and a difficult repair becomes possible.
days.context: Unable to leave the valley, Merrymind returns to the empty cottage and at last meets the mysterious night-spinners.
days.contentNote: A “fagot” here means a bundle of sticks.

excerpt.locator: Merrymind — The Night-Spinners’ Gift; begins “"Merrymind was glad to run the whole way for …” and ends “… blithe and pleasant tune which the night-spinners sang together.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Merrymind suddenly realise these visitors may help his fiddle?
facilitatorNotes: They spin at night, matching the seller’s unusual condition. The old clue gains meaning when he sees them.
evidence: these must be the night-spinners, whose threads would mend his fiddle

questions.prompt: What do the spinners ask for, and why is it difficult to provide?
facilitatorNotes: They ask for sticks to warm the hearth, but the careful valley people have left very few. He searches through the night.
evidence: scarce a stick could be found

questions.prompt: What does Merrymind do before using the golden threads, and what does that show?
facilitatorNotes: He sets the collected sticks on the hearth first, ready for the spinners’ return. He keeps his side of the exchange even when they are absent.
evidence: first heaped up his fagot on the hearth

days.title: Merrymind — Music in the Tower

questions.prompt: What do the listeners do first when the music reaches them?
facilitatorNotes: They stop their tasks and stand still; dancing comes later. This pause lets them listen before anything else changes.
evidence: every one stood still in their places

questions.prompt: How does the story carry the tune from the open valley to Dame Dreary?

evidence: through the halls and up the tower-stairs

questions.prompt: Which action answers the earlier promise that the valley can change when Dame Dreary dances?
facilitatorNotes: She puts down her distaff and dances; the maids join. A distaff holds fibre for spinning, so setting it down breaks the work routine.
evidence: the dame cast down her distaff, and danced with all her might

days.title: Merrymind — A Valley Free to Play
days.challenge: Move between the tale’s ending and the surrounding palace scene.
days.focus: Restored freedom reaches people who were held or burdened in different ways.
days.context: Merrymind’s music has made Dame Dreary dance. Listen for changes beyond the castle and for the listeners’ reaction when the chair ends its tale.

facilitatorNotes: The gate is removed and the captive soldier is freed. These actions directly undo the earlier restriction on leaving.

questions.prompt: Why is it fitting that Merrymind’s mother is the one relative who learns a tune?
facilitatorNotes: She was the one who encouraged him when others mocked his purchase. The ending connects her early support with participation in his joy.
evidence: except Merrymind's mother
